applications.evidence_summary: Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate is the most used dead-space carrier worldwide: 2022 meta-analysis of 16 studies (917 patients) pooled eradication 92%, reoperation 9%, delayed wound healing 20%, aseptic leakage 12%; a 2026 review of 41 studies found no RCTs. US surgeons mix antibiotics into STIMULAN off-label.
applications.caveats: 'May be used at an infected site' is not an antibiotic-delivery claim; US antibiotic mixing is off-label and the company cannot promote it. Wound leakage from calcium sulfate is a known trade-off.
applications.challenge: A hiring manager will probe whether the rep knows the exact line between 'infected site' labeling and off-label antibiotic loading in the US.

applications.evidence_summary: Single-stage tibial osteomyelitis series (n=42, 88.4% remission at 42.8 months) and 163-patient Chinese cohort with autograft (15.3% recurrence) used antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate; bone-transport docking-site series report new bone around resorbing beads.
applications.caveats: Retrospective, non-comparative.

applications.evidence_summary: Alkayali 2024 (PMID 38371037): 45 US diabetic-foot-osteomyelitis cases with surgeon-mixed calcium-sulfate antibiotic beads; only 20% ulcer-free at 3 months, 29% at 6 months, 42% osteomyelitis recurrence at 12 months, 62% wound drainage, 9% acute kidney injury. Chatzipapas 2020 (PMID 33295248): 25 patients, no benefit of local carriers over debridement plus systemic antibiotics.
applications.caveats: Antibiotic loading is off-label (surgeon-compounded); 'may be used at an infected site' is the only infection language on the label. Diabetic-foot evidence is small and unfavorable; the favorable long-bone data use other carriers.

applications.evidence_summary: Widely used in infected Charcot reconstruction and after partial calcanectomy; no Charcot series found.
applications.caveats: Expert practice; wound drainage from calcium sulfate is the recurring complaint.

applications.evidence_summary: Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate beads are the most common US dead-space filler in bone infection, but the evidence is retrospective series dominated by the lower limb and diabetic foot; no upper-extremity-specific comparative study was found. Biocomposites is now running FDA-pathway trials of a premixed vancomycin-gentamicin version, STIMULAN VG, in diabetic foot osteomyelitis (NCT05539963, n=61) and pressure-ulcer osteomyelitis (NCT06283979, phase II, n=60), with an expanded-access program (NCT06808568).
applications.caveats: Off-label antibiotic mixing in the US; hypercalcemia and wound drainage are the known class complications.

evidence.title: Antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate in clinical treatment of chronic osteomyelitis: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Overall eradication 92%; reoperation 9%, refracture 2%, delayed wound healing 20%, aseptic leakage 12%; tobramycin vs vancomycin+gentamicin loading did not change eradication.

evidence.title: Single-stage treatment of chronic localized tibial osteomyelitis with local debridement and antibiotic-loaded calcium sulfate implantation: 42 patients
evidence.finding: 88.4% infection remission without recurrence at mean 42.8 months; prolonged aseptic drainage in 30%.

evidence.title: Multi-center, single-arm, historically controlled pivotal trial of genex G in surgical treatment of osteomyelitis of the extremities
evidence.finding: Recruiting; Biocomposites' gentamicin-preloaded calcium sulfate aimed at the 888.3046 regulation created by CERAMENT G; primary completion October 2027.

evidence.title: Are biodegradable calcium sulfate antibiotic beads effective and safe adjuvants for diabetic foot osteomyelitis?
evidence.finding: 42% osteomyelitis recurrence at 12 months and 62% wound drainage; authors advise caution pending an RCT.

evidence.title: Local antibiotic delivery systems in the surgical treatment of diabetic foot osteomyelitis: again, no benefit?
evidence.finding: Healing 87.5% systemic only vs 100% PMMA beads vs 87.5% calcium sulfate/hydroxyapatite beads; no difference.

evidence.title: A scoping review on the use of antibiotic-impregnated beads and applications to vascular surgery
evidence.finding: 275 publications on antibiotic beads; only 11 RCTs, all but one at high risk of bias; 94% of papers positive, suggesting publication bias.

evidence.title: Randomized phase II trial of STIMULAN VG with debridement and systemic antibiotics vs standard of care for osteomyelitis in stage IV pressure ulcers
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion December 2026.

evidence.title: Randomized feasibility trial of STIMULAN VG with abbreviated vs full systemic antibiotics for diabetic foot osteomyelitis
evidence.finding: Active, not recruiting; primary completion June 2025; results not yet posted.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG; in outpatient settings packaged into the procedure APC.
bd.notes: Biocomposites sells direct in the US (Wilmington, NC subsidiary) and via distributors elsewhere; Stimulan is the value alternative to Cerament G in infection cases, with surgeon-mixed antibiotic as the differentiator and the liability.

pipeline.expected_milestone: STIMULAN VG would be the first premixed antibiotic calcium sulfate with a US label; timing unknown

name: BST-CarGel
ownership_history: Developed by BioSyntech (Canada), then Piramal Healthcare (Canada); Smith+Nephew's affiliate took over ownership of all BST-CarGel product and IP assets from Piramal in January 2016 (terms undisclosed; Ry Ortho/BioSpectrum reports).
composition: Chitosan (with glycerol phosphate) solution mixed by the surgeon with the patient's own whole blood and applied over a microfractured defect, forming a clot-stabilizing scaffold.

regulatory.reference: No US PMA located (openFDA PMA search and web summaries 2026-10-23). Approved for use in Australia, Canada and most of Europe per 2016 coverage; CE/Health Canada certificates not read
on_label_indications: Not authorized in the US. Ex-US: adjunct to microfracture for focal femoral condyle cartilage lesions (per trial design and coverage; labeling not read)

applications.evidence_summary: JBJS 2013 RCT (NCT00314236; n=80, 41 BST-CarGel plus microfracture vs 39 microfracture): at 12 months BST-CarGel gave greater lesion filling (92.8% vs 85.2%, p=0.011) and more hyaline-like T2 values (p=0.033); clinical benefit equivalent. 5-year MRI superiority persisted (lesion filling P=0.017) with no WOMAC difference.
applications.caveats: MRI surrogate endpoints, no clinical superiority, single lesion type; US PMA path unresolved; Piramal-funded.

evidence.title: Novel scaffold-based BST-CarGel treatment results in superior cartilage repair compared with microfracture in a randomized controlled trial
evidence.finding: BST-CarGel beat microfracture on lesion filling (92.8% vs 85.2%) and T2 quality at 12 months; clinical outcomes equivalent.

evidence.title: BST-CarGel Treatment Maintains Cartilage Repair Superiority over Microfracture at 5 Years in a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.finding: MRI lesion filling and T2 superiority persisted at 5 years; WOMAC improved equally in both groups.

evidence.title: Follow-up study evaluating the long-term safety and efficacy of BST-CarGel and microfracture repair of the knee
evidence.finding: Extension study; completed 2014.

bd.reimbursement: Ex-US hospital procurement; not marketed in the US.
bd.notes: Unclear whether S+N still actively markets BST-CarGel; US trials (NCT02981355) terminated with n=5.

name: BioCartilage extracellular cartilage matrix
ownership_history: Arthrex product; development and licensing history not verified.
composition: Dehydrated, micronized allogeneic cartilage extracellular matrix (type II collagen, proteoglycans) reconstituted at the table with autologous PRP/ACP and placed over a microfractured defect.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) - classification inferred; Arthrex pages read did not state it
on_label_indications: Allograft cartilage matrix used as an adjunct to marrow stimulation (microfracture) for focal chondral defects; Arthrex materials describe use in knee and other joints. Exact regulatory statement not read.

challenge: A 361 HCT/P is meant for homologous use without combination with other articles; BioCartilage is routinely combined with PRP, which a regulatory reviewer would question. The FDA classification is not stated on the sources read.

applications.evidence_summary: Brusalis 2020 (Knee): 10 patients, microfracture plus BioCartilage plus PRP, 2-year PROs improved (P<.01); MRI at 1 year showed 2 lesions <50% filled, 4 >50%, 2 complete, 2 hypertrophied. An equine model (Fortier 2016) was positive; two small randomized comparisons are registered (NCT02203071 n=25; NCT03696394 n=15) without located results.
applications.caveats: Tiny uncontrolled series; surgeon-investigators with Arthrex ties; microfracture control not randomized in the published human data.

evidence.title: BioCartilage augmentation of marrow stimulation procedures for cartilage defects of the knee: Two-year clinical outcomes
evidence.finding: Significant PRO gains at 2 years; MRI fill variable (2 of 10 <50%, 2 hypertrophied).

evidence.title: BioCartilage Improves Cartilage Repair Compared With Microfracture Alone in an Equine Model of Full-Thickness Cartilage Loss
evidence.finding: Equine study favoring BioCartilage over microfracture alone.

evidence.title: Comparison of BioCartilage Versus Marrow Stimulating Procedure for Cartilage Defects of the Knee
evidence.finding: Completed 2018; no results located.

bd.reimbursement: Facility-supplied allograft; no separate code; commonly bundled with marrow-stimulation procedure.
bd.notes: Positioned as a low-cost, off-the-shelf microfracture upgrade; competing with DeNovo NT, ProChondrix and Cartiform.

name: Cartiform viable chondral allograft
ownership_history: Made by Osiris Therapeutics; exclusive US commercial distribution and sales partnership with Arthrex announced October 2014 (distribution from 2015; initial 8-year term, Osiris FY2014 10-K; the FY2017 10-K calls it an exclusive marketing and sales-representative agreement). Smith+Nephew acquired Osiris in 2019. Current distribution arrangement and market status not verified.
composition: Cryopreserved (-80 C) human hyaline cartilage disc perforated to expose cartilage with intact chondrocytes (viability preserved), growth factors and matrix; may include a subchondral bone layer in the osteochondral version; implanted with fibrin glue or suture.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) (Osiris FY2014 10-K states it believes Cartiform is regulated as an HCT/P under 21 CFR 1271 and section 361 of the PHS Act, and that it is registered as a tissue establishment)
on_label_indications: Allograft for repair of focal chondral defects; Osiris describes it as 'a viable chondral allograft' promoting articular cartilage repair, implanted in a single step

challenge: Viable-cell cartilage allografts marketed as 361 HCT/Ps depend on a minimally manipulated, homologous-use argument that FDA could contest; Osiris's 10-K says so openly.

applications.evidence_summary: Bennett 2021 (Arthrex-consultant authors): retrospective, 12 patients, mean 2.1 years, IKDC 72.6, KOOS pain 83.8, MOCART reported; a 2025 retrospective patellar cohort (n=65 knees, 50 months) found Cartiform/PJAC without subchondral drilling outperformed drilling plus scaffolds (IKDC 81 vs 74).
applications.caveats: Small retrospective series, no randomized trial found, company-affiliated authors.

evidence.title: Cartiform Implantation for focal cartilage defects in the knee: A 2-year clinical and magnetic resonance imaging follow-up study
evidence.finding: 2-year PROs moderate-good (IKDC 72.6, KOOS pain 83.8) with MOCART assessment.

evidence.title: Cartilage Scaffolds Implanted Without Subchondral Drilling Are Associated With Improved Outcomes and Fewer Complications Compared to Scaffolds Implanted With Subchondral Drilling
evidence.finding: Patellar lesions: no-drilling group (Cartiform 70.6% or PJAC) had higher median IKDC (81 vs 74, P<.001) and fewer complications.

bd.reimbursement: Facility-supplied allograft; no separate payment.
bd.notes: S+N holds Osiris legacy products; Arthrex distribution agreement status after the 2019 acquisition not confirmed.

name: DeNovo NT Natural Tissue Graft (particulated juvenile articular cartilage allograft)
ownership_history: Marketed by Zimmer Orthobiologics (Zimmer Biomet) since 2007 per Zimmer; a Zimmer-listed study identifier references ISTO (ISTO Technologies developed the technology) but the licence/acquisition terms were not verified.
composition: Minced (particulated) hyaline cartilage from juvenile (<13 years) human donors, implanted into a prepared defect and held with fibrin glue; single-stage, no harvest.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) - 361 status is Zimmer's and the literature's characterization; not stated on the pages read
on_label_indications: Homologous use as an allograft for repair of articular cartilage in focal defects (knee, ankle, hip, shoulder per Zimmer materials)
Zimmer describes it as a 'juvenile cartilaginous allograft tissue intended to provide surgeons with an early-intervention option for the repair of articular cartilage' (brochure)

applications.evidence_summary: Farr 2014: 25 patients, 2-year prospective case series (Zimmer-employed co-author): significant gains in IKDC, KOOS and VAS and MRI fill; Zimmer-sponsored post-market registries (NCT00791245 n=25; NCT01329445 n=160; NCT01670617 n=90) have no peer-reviewed full report located. No randomized trial.
applications.caveats: Case series; manufacturer-sponsored; no comparator; 5-year survival figures (85% knee, 89% ankle) appear only in Zimmer materials.
applications.challenge: Because it is a 361 HCT/P with no premarket efficacy review, expect payers and surgeons to ask for comparative data that does not exist.

applications.evidence_summary: Systematic review (2024, 12 studies, 241 patients, 29 months): AOFAS 58.5 to 83.9 but MOCART poor (48.2), complication rate 25.2% (mostly graft hypertrophy), failure 12.4%; authors state PJCA cannot currently be recommended for large OLTs. Zimmer ankle LDC study NCT01347892 (n=205) unreported.
applications.caveats: Review of low-level studies; large lesions fare worse.

evidence.title: Clinical, Radiographic, and Histological Outcomes After Cartilage Repair With Particulated Juvenile Articular Cartilage: A 2-Year Prospective Study
evidence.finding: Significant 2-year improvement in IKDC, KOOS and VAS with progressive MRI defect fill; a co-author is a Zimmer Orthobiologics employee.

evidence.title: Particulated juvenile cartilage allograft for the treatment of osteochondral lesions of the talus is associated with a high complication rate and a high failure rate at short-term follow-up: a systematic review
evidence.finding: AOFAS 58.5 to 83.9, MOCART 48.2, complications 25.2%, failures 12.4%; not recommended for large OLTs.

evidence.title: Post Market Study of Articular Cartilage Defects of the Knee Treated With DeNovo NT, Natural Tissue Graft
evidence.finding: Registry record of the study behind the 2014 report; completed 2012-08.

evidence.title: DeNovo NT Ankle Longitudinal Data Collection Study
evidence.finding: Post-market ankle data collection (status unknown); no publication located.

bd.reimbursement: No pass-through; allograft supply cost sits with the facility; billed in the outpatient cartilage-repair procedure (specific coding per Zimmer coding guide not read).
bd.notes: Zimmer Biomet competes on single-stage convenience against MACI; no independent comparative data exist. Site for ongoing sports-med portfolio (cartilage line also includes Cartiform rivals BioCartilage and ProChondrix).

name: Fresh osteochondral allograft (JRF Ortho)
ownership_history: JRF Ortho is the orthopedic arm of the Joint Restoration Foundation (non-profit tissue bank, Centennial, CO); it states it offers fresh grafts through a member relationship with AlloSource and Community Tissue Services. Arthrex says it partners with JRF Ortho and LifeNet Health to source fresh cartilage allografts.
composition: Fresh (never frozen) human osteochondral dowel or shell grafts with viable chondrocytes, typically transplanted 14-35 days after donor recovery.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) - classification is the standard one for fresh minimally manipulated OCA but was not stated on the JRF pages read
on_label_indications: Allograft osteochondral transplant for focal cartilage and osteochondral defects (homologous use); no label text read

challenge: JRF's sponsored Becker's piece calls fresh OCA 'FDA-approved', which is a promotional misstatement: fresh OCA is a 361 HCT/P with no premarket approval.

applications.evidence_summary: Bulk fresh OCA (JBJS 2021, n=244 knees, mean 9.0 years): survivorship 86.6% at 5 y, 73.3% at 10 y, 58.1% at 15 y, 38% failed; femoral condyle FOCA with realignment osteotomy (BJJ 2019, n=60): 87% at 5 y, 75% at 15 y. Long-term single-center series with no randomized comparison.
applications.caveats: Retrospective single-center registries from tertiary centers; applies to fresh grafts generally, not specifically to JRF-sourced tissue; outcomes worse for medial or multiple grafts and older patients.

applications.evidence_summary: Systematic review (12 studies, 191 patients, mean 57 months): significant AOFAS and VAS gains, 21.6% needed minor secondary procedures; midterm series (Foot Ankle Int 2019) supports use in large cystic talar lesions.
applications.caveats: Case series; graft collapse and fragmentation in large lesions; fresh-graft logistics limit use.

evidence.title: Outcomes of Bulk Fresh Osteochondral Allografts for Cartilage Restoration in the Knee
evidence.finding: Survivorship 86.6% at 5 y, 73.3% at 10 y, 58.1% at 15 y; 38.1% of grafts failed at mean 11 years.

evidence.title: Long-term results of fresh osteochondral allografts and realignment osteotomy for cartilage repair in the knee
evidence.finding: Survivorship 87.3% at 5 y, 74.8% at 15 y, 59.8% at 25 y; malalignment predicted failure.

evidence.title: Fresh Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus: A Systematic Review
evidence.finding: AOFAS and VAS improved significantly across 12 studies; 21.6% minor reoperations.

bd.reimbursement: Tissue fee billed by tissue bank to facility; procedure paid under the facility's outpatient/inpatient arrangement; no separate code.
bd.notes: Hospital-supplied fresh graft with a short shelf life and scheduling constraints; frozen/cryopreserved products (ProChondrix, Cartiform) trade viability for convenience.

name: Fresh osteochondral allograft program (MTF Biologics)
ownership_history: MTF Biologics (formerly Musculoskeletal Transplant Foundation, Edison, NJ; non-profit).
composition: Fresh human osteochondral allografts. The program, grafts offered and handling details were not confirmed from an MTF source in this sweep.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) (assumed, as for other fresh OCA programs; not confirmed)
on_label_indications: Homologous-use osteochondral allograft; no MTF label or brochure was read

challenge: Existence and scope of MTF's fresh OCA offering could not be confirmed from an MTF primary source; a LifeNet FAQ only lists MTF among competitors. Treat as a placeholder pending verification.

applications.evidence_summary: Same class evidence as JRF fresh OCA (see jrf-ortho-fresh-oca record): bulk FOCA of the knee 5-year survivorship 86.6% (n=244). No MTF-specific outcome study located.
applications.caveats: Class evidence only; product-specific data absent.

applications.evidence_summary: Class evidence from fresh OCA of the talus (systematic review of 191 patients); no MTF-specific study located.
applications.caveats: Class evidence only.

evidence.title: Outcomes of Bulk Fresh Osteochondral Allografts for Cartilage Restoration in the Knee
evidence.finding: Class evidence cited for fresh OCA; graft survivorship 86.6% at 5 y.

evidence.title: Fresh Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus: A Systematic Review
evidence.finding: Class evidence cited for fresh OCA of the talus.

bd.reimbursement: Not verified.
bd.notes: Placeholder record: sizing and tissue-bank competition (JRF Ortho, LifeNet Health, AlloSource) not sourced.

name: MACI (autologous cultured chondrocytes on porcine collagen membrane); MACI Arthro
ownership_history: Carticel (first-generation ACI) BLA 1997; MACI developed at Genzyme Biosurgery (EU/Australia sales from 2001-2002); Vericel (then Aastrom Biosciences) acquired the Genzyme cell-therapy business in 2014. MACI EU authorization June 2013, marketing suspended September 2014, manufacturing authorization expired June 2018 (Vericel FY2025 10-K).
composition: Autologous chondrocytes expanded from the patient's own cartilage biopsy and seeded onto a resorbable Type I/III porcine-derived collagen membrane; two-stage procedure (arthroscopic biopsy, then implantation). MACI Arthro is the same implant delivered arthroscopically with custom instruments (a secondary summary of Vericel materials says accessible defects up to 4 cm2; not confirmed in label text read).

regulatory.reference: BL 125603 (STN 125603); original approval 2016-12-13; sBLA approved August 2024 adding arthroscopic delivery instructions
on_label_indications: MACI is an autologous cellularized scaffold product indicated for the repair of symptomatic, single or multiple full-thickness cartilage defects of the knee with or without bone involvement in adults
Label: effectiveness in joints other than the knee has not been established; safety and effectiveness in patients over 55 not established (per FDA label summary on Drugs.com, 7/2022 version)
August 2024 sBLA adds instructions for arthroscopic delivery (Vericel FY2025 10-K)

applications.evidence_summary: SUMMIT (NCT00719576, n=144, 14 European sites) randomized MACI vs microfracture in defects >=3 cm2: co-primary KOOS pain/function improved more with MACI at 2 years (pain 37.0 to 82.5 vs 35.5 to 70.9; function 14.9 to 60.9 vs 12.6 to 48.7; P=.001), and the advantage held on the co-primary at 5 years (P=.022) in the 128-patient extension.
applications.caveats: Sponsor (Genzyme/Sanofi) funded; open-label; MRI and histology showed no between-arm difference in repair-tissue quality; the label is broader (single or multiple defects, with or without bone) than the SUMMIT population (Outerbridge III-IV, >=3 cm2, KOOS pain <55). MACI Arthro approval rested on a delivery-method sBLA, not a new randomized efficacy trial.

applications.evidence_summary: Ankle use is off-label (label limited to the knee). Two Foot Ankle Int series from one center: 20 patients at 21 months (AOFAS 60 to 87) and 15 of those at 12.9 years (AOFAS 60 to 84, MOCART 65). Vericel's randomized MASCOT Phase 3 (NCT06915233, planned n=309, MACI vs arthroscopic marrow stimulation in the talus) began under an IND.
applications.caveats: Small single-center case series; authors note results do not appear superior to established methods at higher cost and two operations; most ankle MACI cases need malleolar osteotomy.

evidence.title: Matrix-Applied Characterized Autologous Cultured Chondrocytes Versus Microfracture: Two-Year Follow-up of a Prospective Randomized Trial (SUMMIT)
evidence.finding: MACI improved KOOS pain and function more than microfracture at 2 years (P=.001); structural repair on histology/MRI was similar.

evidence.title: Matrix-Applied Characterized Autologous Cultured Chondrocytes Versus Microfracture: Five-Year Follow-up of a Prospective Randomized Trial
evidence.finding: The 2-year KOOS advantage for MACI was maintained at 5 years on the co-primary endpoint (P=.022); no new safety signals.

evidence.title: Superiority of MACI versus microfracture in symptomatic articular cartilage defects of the knee (SUMMIT registration)
evidence.finding: Registry record of the pivotal trial; completed March 2012 with posted results.

evidence.title: Matrix-Induced Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation (MACI) Grafting for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus (12.9-year follow-up)
evidence.finding: AOFAS improved from 60 to 84 at about 13 years; MOCART 65 did not correlate with function.

evidence.title: Matrix-Induced Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation (MACI) grafting for osteochondral lesions of the talus (21-month follow-up)
evidence.finding: AOFAS improved from 60 to 87 at a mean 21 months; two failures and four hardware removals.

evidence.title: MASCOT: MACI vs arthroscopic bone marrow stimulation in the talus, ages 17-65 (Phase 3)
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion estimated July 2030. Vericel's 10-K states the trial was initiated in Q4 2025; the registry lists a 2026-05 start date.

evidence.title: MACI in patients aged 10 to 17 with symptomatic chondral or osteochondral defects of the knee (Phase 3)
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion estimated February 2030. Pediatric extension of the knee label.

pipeline.expected_milestone: MACI Ankle (MASCOT) primary completion est. July 2030; pediatric knee study est. February 2030 (ClinicalTrials.gov). UK authorization sought (Vericel FY2025 10-K).

bd.reimbursement: Biopsy plus implant is a two-stage outpatient procedure; the cell product is supplied by Vericel per patient. Per Vericel's 10-K, a vast majority of the largest US commercial payers have a medical policy covering MACI and others approve case by case; specific HCPCS/billing codes not verified here.
bd.notes: Q2 2025 MACI net revenue $53.5M (+21% YoY; Q2 2025 press release). 10-K: company estimates ~750,000 US knee cartilage repair procedures a year, ~315,000 consistent with the label, ~60,000 likely to secure authorization for MACI (company estimates). Target surgeons expanded from 5,000 to 7,000; >900 surgeons trained in MACI Arthro; new Burlington, MA facility approved in 2026 for commercial manufacturing. Company-sourced figures.

name: ProChondrix CR (cryopreserved viable cartilage allograft)
ownership_history: AlloSource (Centennial, CO; non-profit tissue processor). AlloSource and Stryker launched a cryopreserved osteochondral allograft in April 2018; Stryker lists AlloSource ProChondrix in its sports-medicine catalog (distribution terms not read).
composition: Cryopreserved human osteochondral allograft with viable chondrocytes (AlloSource reports mean post-thaw viability about 95% vs 98.8% fresh), supplied as a thin, laser-etched cartilage-on-bone graft and stored frozen.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) - AlloSource's 2025 ICRS poster says ProChondrix CR is regulated under 21 CFR Part 1271; the 361 designation itself was not stated on pages read
on_label_indications: Allograft for repair of articular cartilage defects of the knee (homologous use); company clinical studies cover femoral condyle and patella lesions

applications.evidence_summary: Mehta 2022: 18 patients with ProChondrix thin laser-etched graft plus marrow stimulation, mean 2.5 years: VAS 6.55 to 2.55, IKDC 37.6 to 59.7; 2 reoperations. AlloSource-sponsored prospective study NCT03873545 (n=34) and PACE registry NCT04301258 (n=48, terminated) have no peer-reviewed full report located; AlloSource's 2025 ICRS poster reports through 60 months (company).
applications.caveats: Small single-center series, no control; sponsor data are posters; cryopreserved-viability claims are company research.

evidence.title: Short term clinical outcomes of a Prochondrix thin laser-etched osteochondral allograft for the treatment of articular cartilage defects in the knee
evidence.finding: Pain and IKDC improved significantly at a mean 2.5 years; two failures needed reoperation.

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of ProChondrix CR for Repair of Articular Cartilage Defects on Femoral Condyle and Patella
evidence.finding: Active, not recruiting; primary completion estimated 2028-11.

evidence.title: ProChondrix CR Articular Cartilage Restoration Evaluation (PACE) Registry
evidence.finding: Terminated 2023-09.

bd.reimbursement: Facility-supplied allograft; no separate payment.
bd.notes: Stryker sports-medicine reps distribute AlloSource cartilage products under a 2018 partnership; AlloSource also supplies Stryker GraftJacket (see graftjacket record, processor claim unverified).

name: Spherox (chondrosphere)
ownership_history: co.don GmbH (Leipzig, Germany), marketing authorization holder per EMA EPAR. Authorized 10 July 2017 (CHMP opinion 18 May 2017).
composition: Spheroids of human autologous matrix-associated chondrocytes (EMA active-substance description); applied to the defect without a membrane scaffold (technique details not verified).

regulatory.reference: EU centralized marketing authorization (ATMP) 2017-07-10; not FDA-approved
on_label_indications: Repair of symptomatic articular cartilage defects of the femoral condyle and patella of the knee (ICRS grade III or IV) with defect sizes up to 10 cm2 in adults (EMA EPAR page); the overview also allows skeletally mature adolescents

applications.evidence_summary: Phase III RCT NCT01222559 (n=102: spheroid ACI n=52 vs microfracture n=50, 1-4 cm2 lesions): non-inferior overall KOOS at 24 months and superior on ADL (24 months) and QoL (12 months); 36-month superiority on activity subscores reported in follow-up.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded; open-label; modest defect size; not available or authorized in the US (US evidence status: investigational).

evidence.title: A Prospective, Randomized, Open-Label, Multicenter, Phase III Noninferiority Trial to Compare the Clinical Efficacy of Matrix-Associated Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation With Spheroid Technology Versus Arthroscopic Microfracture for Cartilage Defects of the Knee Joint
evidence.finding: Spheroid ACI met non-inferiority to microfracture on overall KOOS at 24 months; ADL subscore superior.

evidence.title: Matrix-Associated Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation with Spheroid Technology Is Superior to Arthroscopic Microfracture at 36 Months Regarding Activities of Daily Living and Sporting Activities
evidence.finding: 36-month follow-up of the Phase III trial favoring spheroid ACI on ADL and sports (abstract not read in full).

bd.reimbursement: EU hospital/ATMP reimbursement; not US.
bd.notes: One of the few EU ACI products still authorized after ChondroCelect and EU MACI exits.

name: AlloFuse Select CM Cellular Allograft Matrix
ownership_history: AlloSource (non-profit tissue bank, Centennial, CO) processes and sells directly. Brochure M8S0130.001 dated 08/2017.
composition: Moldable, compactable granulated matrix of demineralized bone matrix with native viable bone-forming cells, frozen (1, 5, 10 cc). Company claims (white paper, data on file): on average 3 million viable cells per cc, 85% viability, 68% of cells MSCs; up to 6 hours working time.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER); the AlloFuse 510(k)s in openFDA (K071849 gel/putty, K103036 Plus) are AlloSource's non-cellular DBM devices, not this product
on_label_indications: No indication statement in the brochure read; positioned as a bone graft for fusion sites (361 homologous use). IFU not located.

challenge: The 2017 brochure supports its cell claims with papers on another company's product (Neman 2013 lineage mapping and Baboolal 2014 MSC abundance, both on MTF/Orthofix Trinity Evolution) and cites '25 peer-reviewed clinical papers and 250,000 surgical cases' as data on file. Current availability could not be confirmed (allosource.org blocked automated access).

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of AlloFuse Select CM located (PubMed search 'AlloFuse' 2026-10-23 returned nothing).
applications.caveats: Marketing claims of 'similar clinical outcomes as autograft' are not supported by any product-specific study.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Class payer position: experimental/unproven (Aetna CPB 0411, UHC 2026).

applications.evidence_summary: AlloSource markets to foot and ankle; no study of this product in hindfoot fusion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Tier reflects unconfirmed foot-and-ankle uptake.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs (inpatient) or packaged into the procedure APC (outpatient).
bd.notes: AlloSource also sells non-cellular AlloFuse DBM (existing record allofuse). No FDA warning letter about this product found in the sources read.

name: ArthroCell / ArthroCell Plus Bone Allograft
ownership_history: Arthrex orthobiologics line; processor not named on the product page read.
composition: 100% human-derived viable bone matrix marketed as 'osteogenic, osteoinductive, and osteoconductive', with a DMSO-free cryoprotectant that needs no rinsing or decanting (Arthrex product page). Cell counts and processor not published on the page read.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P); no 510(k) in openFDA for 'arthrocell' (searched 2026-10-23); processor and its CBER registration not identified
on_label_indications: Product page describes use in 'a wide array of orthopedic and spinal applications'; IFU not read

challenge: Arthrex is also the US distributor whose promotional videos for Celularity's Interfyl drew FDA's December 2025 warning letter (see interfyl record); the same promotional-review exposure applies to any 'osteogenic' cellular claim it makes. DMSO-free language mirrors the VIVEX family but the processor is unconfirmed.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of ArthroCell located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Arthrex's foot-and-ankle and sports channel is the likely route; launch year not found.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in nonunion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: None beyond class caveats.

applications.evidence_summary: Page cites spinal applications; no published spine study of ArthroCell located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Arthrex has a small spine presence.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged into the procedure APC in outpatient/ASC cases; bundled in MS-DRG inpatient.
bd.notes: Arthrex sells through a large agency/direct hybrid network. No FDA letter about ArthroCell found in the sources read.

name: BIO4 viable bone matrix
company: Stryker (manufactured by Osiris Therapeutics, a Smith+Nephew company)
ownership_history: Osiris Therapeutics developed the viable bone matrix (marketed earlier as OvationOS). Osiris announced an exclusive worldwide commercialization agreement with Stryker in December 2014 (Osiris manufactures and does research; Stryker markets); Stryker launched BIO4 at AAOS in March 2015. Smith+Nephew completed its acquisition of Osiris on 2019-04-17, so a Stryker competitor's subsidiary manufactures BIO4. Stryker's US spine and trauma/foot-and-ankle BIO4 pages, checked 2026-10-22, still state 'BIO4 is manufactured by Osiris Therapeutics, Inc.'; Smith+Nephew's FY2025 Form 20-F does not discuss BIO4 or the Stryker agreement, and the agreement's current term and renewal terms are not public.
composition: Viable bone matrix containing endogenous bone-forming cells, cancellous bone and demineralized bone; 1-10 cc sizes

regulatory.reference: Section 361 HCT/P (21 CFR 1271)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: Single-center 1-2 level ACDF study with BIO4 in an allograft spacer (NCT03077204, Seton Healthcare, n=20) completed 2020; publication not retrieved. A 2021 systematic review listed one ongoing BIO4 trial and no published BIO4 spine series.
applications.caveats: Weakest published evidence among the major cellular allografts.

applications.evidence_summary: Stryker's Trauma & Extremities page links a 'BIO4: high-energy pilon fractures' case resource; no peer-reviewed foot/ankle study was found.
applications.caveats: Marketing case material only.

applications.evidence_summary: No published foot/ankle series found in PubMed searches for this sweep.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap.

evidence.title: Clinical and radiographic outcomes of BIO4 bone matrix in 1 or 2-level ACDF
evidence.finding: Completed January 2020; no results posted.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Stryker direct spine and trauma reps; supply dependency on a Smith+Nephew subsidiary is a structural oddity worth asking about in any Stryker biologics conversation. Confirmed 2026-10-22: Stryker still lists BIO4 on its US spine and trauma pages with Osiris named as manufacturer; terms of the Stryker-Osiris agreement after the Smith+Nephew deal are not in any public filing found.

challenge: BIO4 is listed as a current Stryker bone grafting product on stryker.com (2026-10-22), which supports the Stryker-Osiris arrangement continuing; the contract itself was not seen.
catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: Cellular bone allografts (CBAs) as a class: comparative evidence, payer position and safety record
company: Multiple (Orthofix/MTF, Globus, LifeNet/DePuy Synthes, Stryker/Osiris, Xtant, VIVEX and its private labels, AlloSource, Highridge, Isto and others; see individual records)
ownership_history: Category began with Osteocel (2005) and Trinity (2009); by 2021 an Orthofix-consultant timeline listed about 20 brands (Osteocel, Trinity Matrix/Evolution/ELITE, Osteocel Plus/Pro, Cellentra, Ovation OS/Bio4, PrimaGen, OsteoVive, V92, VIA Graft, ViviGen, map3, ViaCell, Orios, AlloFuse Select CM, ViBone, SCYLLA, FiberCel). Withdrawals since: map3 (2018), FiberCel (2021), NuCel (2021), ViBone and all Aziyo VBM (2023); PureGen earlier (2013).
composition: Cryopreserved (or, for Virtuos Lyograft, lyophilized) cancellous bone with retained donor cells, usually mixed with demineralized cortical bone; claimed cell content ranges from about 150,000 to over 3,000,000 cells per cc, with processors variously emphasising MSCs (Osteocel, AlloFuse Select CM) or lineage-committed bone-forming cells (ViviGen). Cryoprotectant is DMSO-based (Trinity, ViaCell) or DMSO-free (VIVEX family, ArthroCell).

regulatory.reference: none (each processor self-determines 361 status under 21 CFR 1271.10(a); no FDA premarket review; no CBA has a 510(k), PMA or BLA)
on_label_indications: Homologous use as bone graft / bone void filler for musculoskeletal defects (typical IFU wording: 'treatment of musculoskeletal defects' or 'intended for use as a bone void filler')

challenge: FDA has written to this space more than the 'no warning letters to major CBA makers' line suggests: an untitled letter to Parcell Laboratories over PureGen (June 2011), a Warning Letter to RTI over map3 (November 2017; see map3 record), Organogenesis's own 2021 suspension of NuCel as needing a BLA, and the December 2025 Interfyl letter holding a manufacturer responsible for distributor marketing. The criterion-4 tension (products sold on their living cells must not depend on cell metabolic activity for their primary function) is unresolved. FDA's September 2023 safety communication noted there is no FDA-approved donor screening test for active or latent TB; the IFUs read in this sweep (ViaCell 2021, Viable Matrix Plus 2025) list no M. tuberculosis test.

applications.evidence_summary: Buttermann 2026 randomized single-blinded trial (n=175 in the paper) of six posterior graft options in 1-level anterior/posterior fusion: posterior fusion 98% iliac crest, 94% BMP, 85% marrow aspirate, but only 62-67% with three allograft-MSC products (bone-marrow-, adipose- and amnion-derived) vs 50% for historical plain allograft; outcomes similar if the interbody fused.
applications.caveats: Single surgeon; commercial products not named in the abstract; historical (not randomized) allograft control; trial registered retrospectively (NCT07187362, 119 enrolled vs 175 reported).

applications.evidence_summary: Okonkwo 2026 systematic review (22 studies 2010-2025, no RCTs): lumbar fusion 82-100%, but no study showed a significant improvement over cell-free allograft or other controls; CBAs cost more than cell-free grafts and less than rhBMP-2. Nolte 2026 matched cohort found no fusion gain from PrimaGen added to rhBMP-2 at 80% higher graft cost.
applications.caveats: Heterogeneous fusion assessment, many single-arm sponsor series; UHC cites ECRI 2022 assessments rating lumbar CBA evidence 'inconclusive and very low quality'.

applications.evidence_summary: Zakko 2023 matched retrospective ACDF (34 vs 34): ViviGen vs DBM, no difference in fusion at 3, 6 or 12 months. Okonkwo 2026 review: cervical fusion 90-98.5% across 9 studies, none superior to cell-free controls.
applications.caveats: ECRI 2022 (cited by UHC): cervical CBA evidence very low quality.

applications.evidence_summary: Foot Ankle Int 2022 retrospective comparison of 199 forefoot, midfoot and hindfoot arthrodeses: fusion 93% viable cellular allograft (n=81) vs 86% autograft (n=87) vs 84% combined (n=31), P=0.20, no difference in time to fusion or revision. A DePuy-funded prospective CT study (Park 2024, 14 patients, 30 joints) found 76.7% CT union, 50% at the talonavicular joint.
applications.caveats: Retrospective comparison; CT union rates run well below radiographic rates in the same category.

applications.evidence_summary: Single-site retrospective series of Trinity ELITE in 22 patients with nonunion risk factors: 95% fused at 12 months, 100% in those with prior failed fusion, nicotine use, diabetes, neuropathy or osteoporosis.
applications.caveats: Small, uncontrolled; 'risk for nonunion' is not established nonunion.

evidence.title: Do Cellular Allografts Improve Spinal Fusion Enough to Justify Their Cost and Potential Risk? A Systematic Review of Efficacy, Safety, and Cost
evidence.finding: Systematic review (no pooled meta-analysis) of 22 studies: no RCTs; high reported fusion rates but no study showed superiority over cell-free allograft; two TB outbreaks noted; CBAs costlier than cell-free grafts, cheaper than rhBMP-2.

evidence.title: Comparison of posterior cellular bonegraft options for single-level lumbar spinal fusion: a randomized trial
evidence.finding: Allograft-MSC grafts gave 62-67% posterior fusion vs 98% iliac crest and 94% BMP; cellular allografts had a high cost relative to fusion rate.

evidence.title: Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusions Supplemented With Cellular or Noncellular Allografts Have Similar Radiographic Fusion and Clinical Outcomes
evidence.finding: Matched ACDF cohorts (ViviGen vs DBM in PEEK cages): no difference in motion or bridging-bone fusion at 3, 6 or 12 months; PROMs similar except EQ-5D and PROMIS-physical.

evidence.title: Comparing Rates of Fusion and Time to Fusion in Viable Cellular Allograft and Autograft
evidence.finding: Foot and ankle arthrodeses: fusion 93% viable cellular allograft vs 86% autograft vs 84% combined (P=0.20); no difference in time to fusion or nonunion revision.

evidence.title: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes After Hindfoot and Ankle Arthrodesis Using Cellular Bone Allograft Augmentation: A Short Report
evidence.finding: CT-verified union 76.7% of joints (23/30): ankle 2/2, talonavicular 5/10, calcaneocuboid 8/8, subtalar 8/10.

evidence.title: Radiographical outcomes of a cellular based allograft following foot/ankle arthrodesis in patients with risk for non-union
evidence.finding: Trinity ELITE as primary graft: 21 of 22 patients (95%) fused at 12 months, mean 6 months; no difference by number of risk factors.

evidence.title: Nationwide tuberculosis outbreak in the USA linked to a bone graft product: an outbreak report
evidence.finding: FiberCel lot: 87 of 113 recipients with TB disease, 8 deaths.

evidence.title: Second Nationwide Tuberculosis Outbreak Caused by Bone Allografts Containing Live Cells - United States, 2023
evidence.finding: ViBone Moldable lot: 5 of 36 recipients with confirmed TB, 2 deaths; product was NAAT-negative before release.

bd.reimbursement: No separate payment: bundled in inpatient fusion MS-DRGs, packaged into OPPS/ASC APCs. Commercial payers that publish policies call the category unproven or experimental: UnitedHealthcare 'Spinal Fusion and Bone Healing Enhancement Products' (2026T0410KK, effective 2026-01-01) lists cell-based allograft products such as MSC products as 'unproven and not medically necessary'; Aetna CPB 0411 lists MSC therapy (AlloStem, Osteocel, Osteocel Plus, Ovation, Trinity Evolution) as experimental for all orthopedic applications including spinal fusion; Cigna 0118 (read via a third-party copy) lists 'allograft materials that undergo enhanced processing to retain and condense inherent cells/growth factors' (Trinity Evolution, Osteocel Plus) as experimental.
bd.notes: Because CBAs are bundled, the payer position bites mainly when hospitals itemize implants or when value-analysis committees ask for evidence; the 2026 Colorado cost study ($9,478 vs $5,252 per case) and the 2026 Vanderbilt review are what a VAC will cite. Processor concentration matters: VIVEX alone appears to supply at least five brands; MTF processes Orthofix's Trinity and Virtuos lines.

name: MAGNUS DMSO-free Viable Cellular Bone Allograft
ownership_history: Royal Biologics launched MAGNUS in early 2020 alongside Cryo-Cord (umbilical cord graft). Processor not named in the launch material read; the description matches the VIVEX VIA line (viable spine-derived cells, DMSO-free cryoprotectant), and trade coverage cites the VIA Graft TLIF series as MAGNUS's clinical support.
composition: Osteoconductive 3D scaffold with cortical and cancellous components, a demineralized bone scaffold with osteoinductive potential, and viable spine-derived cells preserved with a DMSO-free cryoprotectant (LER magazine launch item, 2020).

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; processor's CBER establishment registration not identified); no relevant 510(k) in openFDA ('magnus' returns only GE and Magnus Medical devices, searched 2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: 'For fusion in orthopedics' (launch description); IFU not located

challenge: Processor identity (likely VIVEX) is inferred from matching product language, not confirmed from an IFU. Royal's evidence claim borrows another brand's study.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of MAGNUS located (PubMed search 'Magnus allograft cellular' 2026-10-23). The 75-patient TLIF series Royal cites (Tally 2018) was done with VIA Graft, not MAGNUS.
applications.caveats: Borrowed evidence; private-label status unconfirmed.

applications.evidence_summary: Royal markets to podiatry (launched at a podiatry meeting); no study of this product in hindfoot fusion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Tier reflects unconfirmed uptake.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in MS-DRG (inpatient) or packaged in the APC (outpatient).
bd.notes: Small private orthobiologics company selling through independent distributors (channel inferred). No FDA letter about MAGNUS found in the sources read.

name: OSTEOAMP / OSTEOAMP SELECT Fibers / OSTEOAMP Flowable
ownership_history: Developed by Advanced Biologics LLC; Bioventus acquired the OsteoAMP product line, IP and commercial business in October 2014. Still a Bioventus Surgical Solutions product in the FY2024 10-K (no divestiture).
composition: Allograft bone processed to retain endogenous growth factors (BMP-2, BMP-7, VEGF, TGF-beta per company claims) in fibers, putty, sponge, granule and flowable (cannula-delivered, 2024) formats; donor bone from AATB-accredited, FDA-registered US tissue banks

regulatory.reference: No 510(k) for OsteoAMP in openFDA (device_name OSTEOAMP: no matches). The only Bioventus 510(k) tied to it is K233368 'Allograft Delivery Device (OFAC-C)' (2024-06-25, product code FMF), which clears the cannula for delivering hydrated allograft, not the allograft itself. Bioventus FY2025 10-K: allograft from AATB-certified, FDA-registered US tissue banks; sold only in the US.
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: Bioventus registered an intra-patient RCT of OSTEOAMP SELECT Fibers vs Infuse in lumbar fusion (NCT05405374, n=101, 9 sites, started 2022, status unknown as of this review); no peer-reviewed spine fusion outcome paper retrieved.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap; the Infuse-comparator design, if completed, would be the strongest cellular/allograft dataset.

applications.evidence_summary: No foot/ankle clinical data found; published comparison is TLIF/PLIF vs rhBMP-2 (PMID 38759243). A 2026 rat muscle-pouch study found OsteoAMP failed to form bone histologically (PMID 42774656, from a competitor-affiliated group).
applications.caveats: Classification as 'cellular-allograft' is for atlas grouping; it is a growth-factor-retaining allograft without viable cells. The growth-factor claim is contested in the independent preclinical literature.

evidence.title: OSTEOAMP SELECT Fibers vs Infuse as autograft substitute in lumbar fusion: prospective randomized intra-patient controlled multicenter investigation
evidence.finding: Status unknown; primary completion was planned October 2024.

evidence.title: Comparison of TLIF and PLIF outcomes in patients receiving a novel allograft versus rhBMP-2
evidence.finding: Spine interbody comparison of OsteoAMP vs rhBMP-2; not foot/ankle.

evidence.title: A novel growth factor bioavailability-enhanced allograft for use in craniomaxillofacial bone regeneration
evidence.finding: Athymic rat muscle pouch: OsteoAMP, OsteoFactor and i-FACTOR failed to form bone; cellular allografts formed bone inconsistently.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Bioventus direct Surgical Solutions reps plus an indirect team; two issued US patents expire 2029. K233368 (2024-06-25) clears only the cannula-based Allograft Delivery Device used with OsteoAMP Flowable; do not describe OsteoAMP as 510(k)-cleared.

challenge: OsteoAMP itself is a 361 HCT/P with no premarket review; Bioventus's 2024 'FDA approval' of the cannula delivery system is the K233368 510(k) for the delivery device only.

name: Orios Cellular Bone Allograft (Model XT)
ownership_history: Listed among Spinal Elements' featured biologics in its 2020 S-1 (IPO later withdrawn; company private, backed by Kohlberg). Spinal Elements states it does not manufacture its HCT/Ps and serves as a distributor; the processor is not named.
composition: Viable allogeneic bone matrix; a third-party catalog (not read in full) describes an average of 1.5 million viable osteogenic cells per cc preserved with a non-DMSO cryoprotectant, the same figure Medline uses for the VIVEX-processed Viable Matrix Plus.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; Spinal Elements 2020 S-1: 'we are marketing our HCT/Ps pursuant to Section 361'); no 510(k) in openFDA for 'orios' (searched 2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: Not published in the material read; 361 homologous use as bone graft in spinal fusion

challenge: Processor, cell claims and launch year are unconfirmed; the Ryaby 2021 timeline places Orios on the market in the late 2010s.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of Orios located (PubMed search 'Orios' 2026-10-23 returned only unrelated records).
applications.caveats: Sold alongside Spinal Elements hardware.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: None beyond class caveats.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Biologics were 22.5% of Spinal Elements revenue (about $21.6M) in 2019 per the S-1; Orios sits beside Allos (allograft), Nevos (DBM), Provenda (amniotic) and OssiMend (synthetic). No FDA letter found in the sources read.

name: OsteoVive Plus viable bone allograft
ownership_history: Xtant Medical (Belgrade, MT; formerly Bacterin); Xtant acquired Surgalign's biologics assets (2023) and the nanOss production line from RTI, and sells OsteoSponge, OsteoSelect DBM, 3Demin fibers and OsteoVive Plus.
composition: Viable cell-containing cancellous bone with demineralized bone (Xtant describes OsteoVive Plus as a viable bone allograft)

regulatory.reference: No 510(k) for OsteoVive in openFDA (device_name OSTEOVIVE: no matches). Xtant FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-03-31) describes OsteoVive Plus as a viable bone allograft introduced in 2024 and carries a disease-transmission risk factor for it; 361 HCT/P status is inferred from the 10-K's statement that Xtant's products are HCT/Ps, 510(k)-cleared, or both
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical study retrieved.
applications.caveats: Evidence gap.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; Xtant holds biologics contracts with Vizient, Premier and HealthTrust.
bd.notes: Over 670 independent commissioned sales agents and stocking distributors (10-K FY2024); growing private-label/OEM business, including supplying SimpliGraft and SimpliMax under distributor brands. Representative of the small-cap tissue-based spine biologics tier.

name: Osteocel Plus / Osteocel Pro cellular allograft
ownership_history: Developed by Osiris Therapeutics (Osteocel, 2005); NuVasive acquired the Osteocel business from Osiris in 2008 and launched Osteocel Plus (2009) and Osteocel Pro; Globus Medical completed its merger with NuVasive on 2023-09-01. Globus's FY2025 10-K names Osteocel Plus and Osteocel Pro as its allograft cellular lines, processed in San Antonio, TX and Audubon, PA.
composition: Cancellous bone with retained viable mesenchymal stem and osteoprogenitor cells combined with demineralized bone matrix; Pro is a next-generation formulation with higher cell viability claims

regulatory.reference: Section 361 HCT/P (21 CFR 1271); Globus is FDA-registered and state-licensed as a tissue processor; No Osteocel 510(k)/PMA in openFDA (device_name OSTEOCEL: no matches); Globus FY2025 10-K treats Osteocel Plus and Pro as allograft tissue implants supplied by tissue banks (361 HCT/P status inferred)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 homologous use)

applications.evidence_summary: NuVasive-sponsored prospective multicenter cohort (Eastlack 2014, NCT00942045, n=182, 249 levels): 92% of single-level and 87% of combined 1-2 level segments showed solid bridging at 24 months; no revision for pseudarthrosis.
applications.caveats: Nonrandomized, sponsor-funded; largest cellular allograft dataset in ACDF.

applications.evidence_summary: Retrospective MIS-TLIF series (Ammerman 2012, n=23): 91.3% fusion at 12 months; NuVasive TLIF (NCT00947583, n=19) and PLIF (NCT00941980, n=28) cohorts completed 2012.
applications.caveats: Small, single-surgeon.

applications.evidence_summary: Osteocel Plus was NuVasive's house biologic for XLIF; a 104-patient multicenter XLIF cohort (NCT00948532) completed 2012 and a 51-patient ALIF cohort (NCT00948831).
applications.caveats: Publications for the XLIF/ALIF cohorts not retrieved here.

applications.evidence_summary: No trauma data; all published evidence is spinal fusion.
applications.caveats: Same FDA constraints as Trinity.

applications.evidence_summary: No foot or ankle clinical study found; the product's published evidence is spine (single-level ACDF multi-institutional pseudarthrosis analysis, PMID 34062497).
applications.caveats: Spine-focused franchise; foot/ankle use is extrapolation.

applications.evidence_summary: Spine-positioned product; included only because Globus/NuVasive trauma reps can access it. No upper-extremity data.
applications.caveats: No evidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Single-site blinded RCT (Whitt 2020, 11 subjects, 18 sinuses): Osteocel Plus gave a higher vital bone percentage than conventional corticocancellous allograft at posterior sinus sites at 14 weeks; no difference anteriorly.
applications.caveats: Tiny split-mouth trial, histologic surrogate; 361 tissue used in dentistry on homologous-use grounds; CMS and commercial payers call cellular allografts investigational in spine, and dental use is private pay.

evidence.title: Osteocel Plus cellular allograft in ACDF: clinical and radiographic outcomes from a prospective multicenter study
evidence.finding: Solid bridging in 92% of single-level and 87% of all levels at 24 months; 93% patient satisfaction.

evidence.title: The role of Osteocel Plus as a fusion substrate in minimally invasive instrumented TLIF
evidence.finding: 91.3% of patients and 92.3% of levels fused by 12 months.

evidence.title: Osteocel Plus in XLIF: evaluation of radiographic and patient outcomes
evidence.finding: Completed 2012; 13 sites.

evidence.title: Pseudarthrosis rate following anterior cervical discectomy with fusion using an allograft cellular bone matrix: a multi-institutional analysis
evidence.finding: Multi-institutional ACDF series with Osteocel; spine only.

evidence.title: Efficacy of stem cell allograft in maxillary sinus bone regeneration: randomized controlled clinical and blinded histomorphometric study
evidence.finding: Osteocel Plus produced significantly more vital bone than alloOss allograft at posterior grafted sites (p=0.03) in 18 sinuses; no anterior difference.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; payer policies list Osteocel as investigational for spine fusion.
bd.notes: Globus sells primarily through an exclusive global sales force, with some US reps employed by exclusive independent distributors; Globus relies on several tissue banks for allograft supply and processes Osteocel in-house (former NuVasive facilities).

name: PrimaGen Advanced Allograft
company: Highridge Medical (H.I.G. Capital; former ZimVie / Zimmer Biomet spine business)
ownership_history: Launched by Zimmer Biomet in December 2016; moved to ZimVie at the 2022 spin-off; ZimVie sold its spine business to H.I.G. Capital on April 1, 2024 ($375M), renamed Highridge Medical. The ZimVie PrimaGen product page now returns 404; current listing by Highridge not confirmed.
composition: Fresh-frozen (cryopreserved) cancellous bone with retained viable donor cells plus demineralized cortical bone fibers with verified osteoinductivity, in a pre-filled syringe with a built-in filter. Launch materials claimed at least 750,000 cells per cc of cancellous tissue with at least 70% viability.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P regulated under 21 CFR Part 1271 per launch materials); no 510(k) in openFDA for 'primagen' (searched 2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: 'Intended for homologous use in the repair, replacement, reconstruction or supplementation of recipient tissue' in musculoskeletal defects that are surgically created or result from traumatic bone injury (Zimmer Biomet launch, December 2016)

challenge: The only comparative study is negative on value: Nolte 2026 (University of Colorado, 100 matched patients) found PrimaGen plus rhBMP-2 did not improve interbody fusion over rhBMP-2 plus DBM/allograft and raised osteobiologic cost per case from $5,252 to $9,478. Status flagged unverified after the 2024 sale.

applications.evidence_summary: Nolte 2026 retrospective matched cohort, 1-2 level PLIF/TLIF 2017-2023: fusion 95.7% vs 89.1% at 12 months (P=0.27) and 100% vs 89.5% at 24 months (P=0.49) with PrimaGen plus rhBMP-2 vs rhBMP-2 plus DBM/allograft; higher blood loss and 6-month pain in the PrimaGen arm; cost $9,478 vs $5,252 per case.
applications.caveats: Retrospective, single institution, radiograph-based fusion assessment; both arms got rhBMP-2, so the cellular graft's own effect cannot be isolated.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of PrimaGen in posterolateral fusion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Class payer position: unproven/experimental.

applications.evidence_summary: Label language covers traumatic bone injury defects; no study in fracture or nonunion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Marketed through a spine channel; trauma use unconfirmed.

evidence.title: Role of a Novel, Fresh-Frozen Cellular Bone Allograft in Lumbar Interbody Spinal Fusion: A Retrospective, Matched-Cohort Study
evidence.finding: PrimaGen plus rhBMP-2 vs matched rhBMP-2 plus DBM/allograft: no difference in fusion at 12 or 24 months, revision or complications; higher blood loss and 6-month pain; 80% higher osteobiologic cost per case.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: A Highridge rep would face the Colorado cost data directly. Sponsor_funded set false on the basis of an academic author list; the funding statement was not read in full. No FDA letter about PrimaGen found in the sources read.

name: SCYLLA Cellular Bone Allograft
ownership_history: Camber Spine (King of Prussia, PA) entered the cellular bone graft market in August 2019 through a private-label agreement; the manufacturer is not named in the coverage read. The description (viable spine-derived cells, 4-hour post-thaw window, 2-year shelf life at -65 C or colder, microparticulate blend and moldable pastes) matches the VIVEX VIA line.
composition: Allogeneic bone matrix with viable spine-derived cells: cortical/cancellous microparticulate scaffold, demineralized bone component, bone-derived cells; formats are a blend, a moldable paste and a fibrous moldable paste.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; processor's establishment registration not identified); no 510(k) in openFDA for 'scylla' (searched 2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: No formal indication published in the material read; positioned to complement Camber's SPIRA and ENZA interbody platforms (361 homologous use as bone graft)

challenge: Private label with no disclosed processor and no product-specific data; current availability not confirmed.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of SCYLLA located (PubMed search 'Scylla allograft' 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Bundled with Camber cages; graft choice may follow the hardware sale.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in ALIF located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Camber's SPIRA-A is an ALIF cage; pairing is commercial, not evidence-based.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Example of a hardware company adding a cellular graft to its bag via private label. No FDA letter found in the sources read.

name: Trinity ELITE / Trinity Evolution viable cellular bone allograft
ownership_history: Trinity Evolution launched 2009 (Orthofix/MTF); Trinity ELITE (moldable) 2014; Orthofix holds exclusive worldwide marketing rights and MTF processes, holds inventory and invoices customers, paying Orthofix a marketing service fee ($51.7 million in 2024, ~31% of Orthofix Biologics revenue). The May 2022 renewal runs through 2032. Orthofix and SeaSpine completed their all-stock merger effective 2023-01-05 (SeaSpine survives as an Orthofix subsidiary).
composition: Cryopreserved cancellous bone containing viable mesenchymal stem/osteoprogenitor cells, combined with demineralized cortical bone (ELITE adds demineralized fibers for moldability)

regulatory.reference: Regulated solely under Section 361 PHS Act / 21 CFR 1271 (no premarket review); homologous use as a bone void filler
on_label_indications: Bone void filler for voids or gaps that are not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure (361 HCT/P homologous-use statement)

applications.evidence_summary: Prospective multicenter single-arm studies (NCT00951938): single-level ACDF with Trinity Evolution in a PEEK cage fused 93.5% at 12 months (Vanichkachorn 2016, n=31); two-level ACDF fused 89.4% per subject at 12 months (Peppers 2017, n=40).
applications.caveats: Orthofix-funded, single-arm with historical comparison; a 2021 systematic review found no comparative multicenter trial of any cellular bone matrix free of industry conflicts.

applications.evidence_summary: Orthofix PLIF/TLIF cohort (NCT00965380, n=207) completed 2014; a 300-patient Trinity ELITE lumbar post-market study (NCT02969616) has unknown status. Trinity ELITE is the comparator in Kuros's MagnetOs Flex Matrix PLF RCT (NCT05037968).
applications.caveats: Lumbar results not retrieved as a publication in this sweep.

applications.evidence_summary: Rat PLF model ranked Trinity ELITE highest among cellular matrices (8/15 fused vs 0/15 Osteocel Pro, 2/15 ViviGen; Lin 2020); human PLF comparative data pending NCT05037968.
applications.caveats: Animal data; payer policies (e.g., Blue Cross FEP 8.01.52) list Trinity, Osteocel and ViviGen as investigational for spine fusion.

applications.evidence_summary: PubMed search for Trinity/ViviGen/Osteocel in fracture, nonunion or trauma returned no relevant clinical studies; the evidence base is spine (and some foot-and-ankle fusion). FDA position: a 361 HCT/P may not be marketed with osteoinductive or cell-potency claims, and nonunion use is a homologous-use argument at best.
applications.caveats: Price per cc is the highest in the trauma graft set with no trauma data; the 'viable cells' claim is unproven in fracture healing. Treated as investigational for trauma per the atlas rules.
applications.challenge: A trauma biologics manager will ask for one nonunion study; there is none.

applications.evidence_summary: Jones 2015 (FAI; PMID 25976919; NCT00988338): prospective, multicenter, open-label, single-arm trial of Trinity Evolution in 92 patients (153 joints) with foot and/or ankle arthrodesis; fusion at 12 months 71.1% of patients and 86.8% of joints, with no CBA-attributed adverse events.
applications.caveats: Orthofix-funded with Orthofix employees as authors; predecessor product; no control arm, so the 'comparable to autograft' claim is against historical rates; 16 of 92 patients lost by 12 months.

applications.evidence_summary: Same single-arm trial (PMID 25976919) included subtalar, talonavicular, calcaneocuboid, double and triple fusions.
applications.caveats: As above.

applications.evidence_summary: Donaghue 2024 (PMID 38562146): single-site retrospective series of 22 patients (29 joints) with at least one nonunion risk factor fused with Trinity ELITE; 95% fusion at 12 months.
applications.caveats: Single author, single site, 22 patients, no comparator; cited by Orthofix marketing.

applications.evidence_summary: Marketed into nonunion revision as an autograft replacement; the company's cited studies are all spine (cervical and lumbar fusion). No upper-extremity clinical data found.
applications.caveats: FDA position: a 361 HCT/P may not be labeled or promoted with osteoinductive/osteogenic claims that imply more than minimal manipulation and homologous use; the cell-count claims are manufacturer specifications, not clinical outcomes.

applications.evidence_summary: No evidence; usage anecdotal.
applications.caveats: As above.

applications.evidence_summary: No dental or maxillofacial clinical study of Trinity Elite located on PubMed as of 2026-10-22; Orthofix positions it for general bone grafting and does not market a dental program.
applications.caveats: Listed for completeness; the cellular allograft dental evidence is the Osteocel Plus pilot RCT.

evidence.title: Prospective 12-month outcome study of single-level ACDF using Trinity Evolution with comparison to historical controls
evidence.finding: Fusion 78.6% at 6 months, 93.5% at 12 months; no graft-related serious AEs.

evidence.title: Prospective evaluation of Trinity Evolution in two-level ACDF
evidence.finding: Per-subject fusion 89.4%, per-level 93.4% at 12 months; no revisions.

evidence.title: Existing clinical evidence on the use of cellular bone matrix grafts in spinal fusion: updated systematic review
evidence.finding: 12 studies of 6 products (Osteocel n=354, Trinity n=114, ViviGen n=171, map3 n=41, VIA Graft n=75) all reported 87-100% fusion but were single-center/noncomparative; 7 disclosed industry COI; insufficient evidence to recommend CBMs over cheaper materials.

evidence.title: Prospective, multicenter evaluation of allogeneic bone matrix containing viable osteogenic cells in foot and/or ankle arthrodesis
evidence.finding: 12-month fusion 71.1% per patient and 86.8% per joint with Trinity Evolution; high-risk subgroups fused at similar rates.

evidence.title: Trinity Evolution Matrix in subjects undergoing foot and ankle fusion
evidence.finding: Registry record for the Jones 2015 study; completed January 2013, 10 sites.

evidence.title: Radiographical outcomes of a cellular based allograft following foot/ankle arthrodesis in patients with risk for non-union
evidence.finding: 21 of 22 patients fused by 12 months with Trinity ELITE as the primary graft.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs; +20930 bundled; many commercial payers deem cellular allografts for spine fusion investigational, which can trigger denials when itemized.
bd.notes: Orthofix books marketing-service fees rather than product revenue; MTF is single-source for Trinity and FiberFuse (10-K risk factor). Orthofix distributes biologics globally through distributors and sales representatives; the 2025 Trinity ELITE 'full market release' refers to a relaunch of updated formulations.

name: V92 / V92-FC Cellular Bone Matrix
company: Zimmer Biomet (via Paragon 28, acquired April 21, 2025); processed by VIVEX
ownership_history: Paragon 28 (Englewood, CO, foot and ankle) launched V92 on January 11, 2016; its cell data cite 'data on file at Vivex Biomedical, Inc.' Zimmer Biomet completed its acquisition of Paragon 28 on April 21, 2025. Whether V92 remains in the combined catalog is unconfirmed.
composition: Viable allogeneic bone scaffold with bone microparticulate of 100-300 um in two blends (V92, V92-FC); DMSO-free cryoprotectant with no rinse or decant; company claims >80% post-thaw viability and at least 150,000 viable cells per cc, 4-hour working window, 2-year shelf life at -65 C or colder.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; processor VIVEX registered with CBER); the only openFDA 'V92' 510(k) (K911533) is an unrelated dental alloy
on_label_indications: 'Intended for homologous use as a bone void filler' (Paragon 28 launch release, January 2016)

challenge: A foot-and-ankle-first cellular graft now inside Zimmer Biomet; post-acquisition availability not confirmed (status marked unverified).

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of V92 located (PubMed search 'V92 allograft' 2026-10-23 returned nothing).
applications.caveats: Class evidence in foot and ankle comes from Trinity Evolution and ViviGen series, not V92.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in first MTP fusion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Bone void filler labeling; most first MTP fusions heal without graft.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in revision or nonunion surgery located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: None beyond class caveats.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged into the procedure APC in outpatient/ASC foot and ankle cases; bundled in MS-DRG inpatient.
bd.notes: Paragon 28 sold through a dedicated foot-and-ankle channel; Zimmer Biomet said the deal creates a dedicated foot and ankle sales channel with ASC focus. No FDA letter found in the sources read.

name: VIA Graft / VIA Form / VIA Form+ Viable Bone Matrix
ownership_history: VIVEX Biologics, Inc. (formerly VIVEX Biomedical, Marietta, GA in 2018 publications). VIVEX processes the VIA line and, on the evidence below, private-label viable bone matrices for other brands (Paragon 28 V92 cites 'data on file at Vivex Biomedical'; the Medline Unite Viable Matrix Plus IFU names Vivex as processor; Royal Biologics MAGNUS and Camber Spine SCYLLA use the same 'viable spine-derived cells', DMSO-free, 4-hour, -65 C description). VIVEX also makes VIA Disc NP (existing record via-disc-np).
composition: VIA Graft: 100-300 um demineralized cortical bone with mineralized cortical and cancellous bone; VIA Form: cortical shavings, crushed cancellous chips and 100-300 um demineralized cortical microparticulate; VIA Form+: syringe-delivered demineralized cortical fibers with cancellous chips. Cells are 'viable spine-derived cells' (vertebral body donor bone). Preserved with VIACoat, a DMSO-free extracellular cryoprotectant; company data claim >80% post-thaw viability, 4-hour use window, 3-year storage at -65 C or colder.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER); no 510(k) in openFDA for 'via graft' or 'via form' (searched 2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: Viable bone matrices 'to support bone formation in a variety of bone graft clinical applications' (VIVEX technical update, ISASS 2021); 361 homologous use as bone graft. VIA IFU not located; the sister private-label IFU (Viable Matrix Plus) reads 'intended for use as a bone void filler'.

challenge: One processor, many brands: a buyer comparing MAGNUS, SCYLLA, V92 and Viable Matrix Plus may be comparing the same VIVEX tissue under different labels, and the only peer-reviewed clinical series (Tally 2018) was done with VIA Graft.

applications.evidence_summary: Tally 2018: 75 consecutive MIS-TLIF patients (85 levels) with VIA Graft; 96% fusion at 12 months. A 2026 company-announced retrospective of 14 VIA Form+ interbody fusions (Journal of Spine & Neurosurgery) is not PubMed-indexed and was not read.
applications.caveats: Single-surgeon retrospective case series; two co-authors were VIVEX consultants; no control group.

applications.evidence_summary: VIVEX cites 67 LLIF patients (151 levels, 94.7% fused) as 'data submitted for publication'; no published lateral-fusion study of VIA located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Company data on file only.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in posterolateral fusion located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Class payer position: unproven (UHC 2026) / experimental (Aetna).

evidence.title: Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion With Viable Allograft: 75 Consecutive Cases at 12-Month Follow-up
evidence.finding: 96% of 85 levels fused at 12 months after MIS-TLIF with VIA Graft; no comparison group.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient fusion MS-DRGs; packaged in OPPS when outpatient.
bd.notes: VIVEX sells its own VIA brand and appears to OEM the same tissue to device companies without biologics manufacturing (Royal, Camber, Paragon 28, Medline). DMSO-free storage is the commercial pitch (no rinse or decant). No FDA warning letter to VIVEX about the VIA line found in the sources read.

name: ViaCell Viable Cell Allograft
company: Globus Medical (processed by Bone Bank Allografts, San Antonio)
ownership_history: Supplied by Globus Medical and processed and prepared by Bone Bank Allografts (BBA) per the US package insert (LB-275 R06, 06/2021). Globus merged with NuVasive in 2023, so it now sells both ViaCell and Osteocel.
composition: Partially demineralized cortical fibers and cancellous chips with inherent stem cells and osteoprogenitor cells (Globus product page); packaged in a cryoprotectant of 10% DMSO in MEM-alpha, shipped on dry ice, stored at -40 C or colder. Trace povidone-iodine, vancomycin, meropenem and amphotericin B may remain. Globus does not publish a cell count on the pages read.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER); insert states processed under 21 CFR Part 1271 and AATB standards; no 510(k) in openFDA for 'viacell' (searched 2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: 'This allograft may be used for the treatment of musculoskeletal defects' (ViaCell US insert LB-275 R06, 06/2021)

challenge: The insert's donor-testing list (HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, CMV, optional HTLV) contains no Mycobacterium tuberculosis test, the gap both CDC outbreaks exposed. Launch year not confirmed; an Orthofix-consultant slide deck (Ryaby, 2021) places ViaCell on the market in the late 2010s.

applications.evidence_summary: No published clinical study of ViaCell located (PubMed search 'ViaCell allograft' 2026-10-23 returned only unrelated records).
applications.caveats: Evidence for Globus's cellular line rests on Osteocel, a different product.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Commercial payers (UnitedHealthcare 2026, Aetna CPB 0411) class cell-based allografts as unproven or experimental.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: None beyond the class caveats.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient fusion MS-DRGs; no separate payment.
bd.notes: Second cellular brand in the Globus bag next to Osteocel Pro (Osteocel record: hybrid direct/exclusive-distributor channel). BBA cost-recovery is reimbursed 'in part' by Globus per NOTA. No FDA warning or untitled letter about ViaCell was found in the sources read; FDA's warning-letter database was not searched by company.

name: ViviGen / ViviGen Formable / ViviGen MIS cellular bone matrix
company: LifeNet Health (processor/owner); DePuy Synthes (exclusive worldwide marketer)
ownership_history: Processed and owned by LifeNet Health (Virginia Beach, VA nonprofit tissue bank); LifeNet's own page calls it 'a 361 Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular-based Product'. DePuy Synthes holds an exclusive worldwide agreement to market and promote ViviGen (launched late 2014, full US release January 2015) and ViviGen Formable (2017), per OrthoWorld/Becker's; J&J MedTech still lists 'ViviGen Cellular Bone Matrix' as a DePuy Synthes product in 2026 (the page carries no IFU or processor statement). Terms of the agreement are not public.
composition: Cryopreserved viable lineage-committed bone cells within corticocancellous bone matrix plus demineralized bone; Formable adds a moldable DBM fiber component

regulatory.reference: No premarket number; LifeNet states ViviGen is a 361 HCT/P (21 CFR 1271)
on_label_indications: Bone void filler / repair or reconstruction of musculoskeletal defects (361 homologous use; voids not intrinsic to the stability of the bony structure)

applications.evidence_summary: Matched retrospective cohort (Zakko 2023, n=68): no difference in fusion or PROMs between ViviGen and DBM in 1-4 level ACDF; DePuy's 100-patient 2-3 level ACDF cohort (NCT02814825) completed 2021 (publication not retrieved).
applications.caveats: Only comparative data show equivalence to a much cheaper DBM.

applications.evidence_summary: Investigator-initiated RCT vs local autograft in PLF (NCT03733626, Corewell Health, n=46) completed 2024, results not yet published; an Ohio State single-arm PLF study (NCT04007094) was terminated; a Swiss RCT vs rhBMP-2 in ALIF/XLIF (NCT05238740, n=168) is recruiting to 2032.
applications.caveats: Rat PLF model: ViviGen 2/15 fused vs Trinity ELITE 8/15 (Lin 2020).
