evidence.title: Osteogenic protein-1 (BMP-7) accelerates healing of scaphoid non-union with proximal pole sclerosis
evidence.finding: OP-1 reduced radiographic healing time to 4 weeks vs 9 weeks with autograft alone.

evidence.title: Recombinant human BMP-2 and allograft compared with autogenous bone graft for reconstruction of diaphyseal tibial fractures with cortical defects (BESTT-ALL)
evidence.finding: Lower-limb reference trial: rhBMP-2 plus allograft matched autograft for tibial defects; cited when surgeons extrapolate to the humerus.

evidence.title: Phase 1 dose-escalating study of rhBMP-2/calcium phosphate matrix as adjuvant therapy for closed distal radius fractures
evidence.finding: Safety/feasibility only; no results posted.

evidence.title: Pivotal, randomized, parallel evaluation of rhBMP-2/ACS and autogenous bone graft for maxillary sinus floor augmentation
evidence.finding: rhBMP-2/ACS gave 7.83 mm versus 9.46 mm height with autograft, denser bone, equivalent implant integration (199/241 vs 201/251) at six months after loading, no treatment-related adverse events, and avoided the 17 percent donor-site morbidity of autograft.

evidence.title: De novo bone induction by rhBMP-2 in maxillary sinus floor augmentation (phase II)
evidence.finding: 0.75 and 1.50 mg/mL rhBMP-2/ACS produced ridge height gains of 9.5 and 10.2 mm versus 11.3 mm with bone graft at four months; 1.5 mg/mL chosen for the pivotal trial.

evidence.title: The negative effect of combining rhBMP-2 and Bio-Oss on bone formation for maxillary sinus augmentation
evidence.finding: Histologic new bone was lower with rhBMP-2/ACS plus Bio-Oss than with Bio-Oss alone.

evidence.title: Efficacy of rhBMP-2 and rhPDGF-BB in orofacial bone regeneration: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
evidence.finding: Pooled RCTs show rhBMP-2 and rhPDGF-BB produce orofacial bone gains comparable to conventional grafts without a clear advantage, with dose and indication effects unresolved.

evidence.title: Evaluation of maxillary alveolar reconstruction using a resorbable collagen sponge with rhBMP-2 in cleft lip and palate patients
evidence.finding: Children 8 to 12: rhBMP-2 group reached 65 percent mean bone height at 12 months versus 83.8 percent at 6 months with iliac crest; significant swelling in 37.5 percent of the rhBMP-2 arm versus donor-site pain in 87.5 percent of the ICBG arm.

evidence.title: Human bone morphogenetic protein-2 use for maxillary reconstruction in cleft lip and palate patients
evidence.finding: Formed bone volume, formation rate, height repair and density were similar for rhBMP-2 and iliac crest at one year; periosteoplasty arm abandoned for insufficient bone.

evidence.title: Efficacy of rhBMP-2 in alveolar cleft treatment for children: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Six RCTs and two non-randomized studies: bone volume 61.1 percent with rhBMP-2 versus 59.1 percent with iliac crest, bone height lower with rhBMP-2 (about 61 versus 79 percent), moderate-quality evidence of no significant difference.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of rhBMP-2 versus iliac autogenous bone graft in cleft patients: umbrella review
evidence.finding: Six systematic reviews, bone fill 74.2 percent rhBMP-2 versus 72.4 percent autogenous, none at low risk of bias; recommends caution in children.

evidence.title: rhBMP-2 as an alternative to autologous bone graft in pediatric craniofacial reconstruction: systematic review
evidence.finding: 21 studies (6 RCTs): in alveolar cleft 4 of 12 favored rhBMP-2 for bone formation, 1 favored ICBG, 7 no difference; facial edema the commonest rhBMP-2 complication; all five operative-time studies favored rhBMP-2.

evidence.title: Reconstruction of mandibular continuity defects with rhBMP-2
evidence.finding: 14 body and angle defects from tumor or osteomyelitis regenerated with rhBMP-2 on collagen alone under tenting hardware; all restored to prosthetic function at 6 to 18 months.

evidence.title: Off-label use of rhBMP-2 for reconstruction of mandibular bone defects in humans
evidence.finding: Three of five defects healed; both failures were continuity defects, salvaged with iliac crest.

evidence.title: Safety and efficacy of rhBMP-2 in craniofacial surgery
evidence.finding: 17 RCTs (n 7 to 160) support use in sinus and alveolar settings; evidence fails to support rhBMP-2 for maxillary sinus wall augmentation, calvarial reconstruction, mandibular reconstruction or distraction osteogenesis.

evidence.title: Cost effectiveness in alveolar bone grafting in patients with cleft lip and palate: randomized clinical trial (DBM/BMP vs ICBG)
evidence.finding: Recruiting at UT Health Houston, ages 6 to 15, primary endpoint health-system cost per successful graft at one year; completion 2028.

bd.reimbursement: Inpatient: bundled in the level-based spinal fusion MS-DRG family in force since FY2025 (402, 426-430, 447-451, 456-458; 523-525 added FY2027; 471-473 cervical) and 471-473 (cervical); no separate HCPCS; physician add-on +20930 (osteopromotive material) is a bundled 0-RVU code for Medicare. Payer medical policies commonly cover rhBMP-2 only for on-label lumbar interbody use and deny cervical use.
bd.notes: Priced at several thousand dollars per kit (ISSG mean $14,000 per deformity case); Medtronic's TLIF label (Feb 2026) and Breakthrough designation (Apr 2024) are the first new spine indications since 2018. Kuros MagnetOs is now sold by the Medtronic spine sales force under a 2025 agency agreement, giving Medtronic a non-BMP alternative in the same bag.
bd.challenge: C9359 attribution and current OPPS packaging status for Infuse not re-verified in this sweep.

challenge: FDA's July 1, 2008 Public Health Notification (CDRH, signed Daniel G. Schultz) was retrieved via the Wayback Machine: at least 38 reports over four years of neck/throat swelling with airway compression after cervical rhBMP use, most at 2-14 days; FDA states safety and effectiveness in the cervical spine 'have not been demonstrated' and recommends approved alternatives or enrollment in approved studies. The TLIF supplement is P000058/S096 (panel track, decision 02/13/2026). Remaining gap: Medtronic's release gives only 'fusion rates exceeding 90 percent in single-level TLIF' for Infuse (493 randomized 1:1:1 to 2.1 mg/level, 4.2 mg/level, local autograft; stopped for success at the first interim analysis of 480 treated patients); the autograft-arm and two-level percentages are unpublished.

name: Augment Bone Graft
ownership_history: Developed by BioMimetic Therapeutics (Franklin, TN); BioMimetic acquired by Wright Medical Group 2013; Wright Medical acquired by Stryker (closed November 2020). Stryker still lists Augment Bone Graft and Augment Injectable in its Trauma & Extremities biologics line as of this review; no divestiture found.
composition: Recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor-BB (0.3 mg/mL, yeast-expressed) with beta-tricalcium phosphate granules; drug-device combination product

on_label_indications: As an alternative to autograft in arthrodesis (surgical fusion) of the ankle and/or hindfoot joints in patients with osteoarthritis, post-traumatic, rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, avascular necrosis, joint instability or deformity, congenital defects, or other joint arthropathies, who need supplemental graft material on pre- or intraoperative assessment (summary of the approval order; FDA PMA P100006, decision 2015-09-01)

applications.evidence_summary: DiGiovanni 2013 (JBJS; PMID 23824386): 434 patients at 37 North American sites randomized 2:1 to rhPDGF-BB/beta-TCP or autograft for hindfoot or ankle fusion; CT fusion at 6 months 61.2% of patients (66.5% of joints) vs 62.0% (62.6%), clinical healing at 52 weeks 86.2% vs 87.6%, noninferior with less pain and fewer graft-site complications.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded (BioMimetic); noninferiority design against autograft; absolute 6-month CT fusion rates in the low 60s on both arms; two-thirds of enrolled joints were hindfoot rather than tibiotalar.

applications.evidence_summary: Same pivotal RCT (PMID 23824386); subtalar, talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints made up most of the 597 joints analyzed.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded; no subgroup powered for any single joint.

applications.evidence_summary: Label is for primary arthrodesis; no revision or nonunion trial found.
applications.caveats: Off-label in revision; CMS cited a post-hoc finding that patients 65 and older were more than twice as likely to fuse with Augment than autograft, which has not been prospectively replicated.

evidence.title: Recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor-BB and beta-tricalcium phosphate (rhPDGF-BB/beta-TCP): an alternative to autogenous bone graft
evidence.finding: Noninferior to autograft for hindfoot/ankle fusion on CT at 6 months and clinical healing at 52 weeks, with less pain and fewer side effects.

evidence.title: Prospective, randomized, multi-center feasibility trial of rhPDGF-BB versus autologous bone graft in a foot and ankle fusion model
evidence.finding: Radiographic union 77% Augment vs 50% autograft at 36 weeks in a 20-patient pilot; surgery 26 minutes shorter without harvest.

evidence.title: Pivotal trial of Augment Bone Graft vs autologous bone graft in foot and ankle fusions
evidence.finding: Registry entry for the pivotal trial (enrollment 414 listed; 434 in the publication); completed, primary completion January 2010.

evidence.title: Post-approval trial of Augment Bone Graft vs autologous bone graft in foot and ankle fusions
evidence.finding: FDA-required post-approval study; status listed as unknown on ClinicalTrials.gov, no results posted.

bd.reimbursement: Inpatient: bundled in the MS-DRG. Hospital outpatient and ASC: CMS granted transitional pass-through status under device category C1734 effective 2020-01-01, billed with ankle/hindfoot arthrodesis CPT codes (27870 and related), after finding substantial clinical improvement from eliminating donor-site pain; pass-through lasts two to three years, so the product is now packaged into the procedure APC/ASC rate (exact expiry date not verified in this sweep).
bd.notes: Carried by Stryker Foot & Ankle (ex-Wright) reps alongside Prophecy/Infinity ankle and hindfoot nail systems; the only PMA-approved osteoinductive product with a foot-and-ankle label, which is its core contracting argument against 361 cellular allografts. The pass-through window (2020-2022/23) was the main commercial catalyst after approval.

catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: Augment Injectable Bone Graft
ownership_history: Same chain as Augment Bone Graft: BioMimetic Therapeutics to Wright Medical (2013) to Stryker (2020).
composition: rhPDGF-BB (0.3 mg/mL) with an injectable beta-tricalcium phosphate and bovine type I collagen matrix

on_label_indications: Same indication as Augment Bone Graft: alternative to autograft in ankle and hindfoot arthrodesis (PMA supplement S005, approval notice dated 2018-06-12)

applications.evidence_summary: Daniels 2015 (FAI; PMID 25848134): 75 patients randomized 5:1 (63 Augment Injectable, 12 autograft) plus 142 autograft controls from the parallel Augment trial; complete CT fusion at 24 weeks 84% vs 65% (p<0.001), clinical success at 52 weeks 91% vs 78%.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-funded (Wright Medical author); only 12 concurrent randomized controls, the rest borrowed from a separate trial with an identical protocol; superiority signal rests on that pooled control.

applications.evidence_summary: Same trial (PMID 25848134); NCT01305356 lists 299 enrolled.
applications.caveats: As above.

evidence.title: Prospective randomized controlled trial of hindfoot and ankle fusions treated with rhPDGF-BB in combination with a beta-TCP-collagen matrix
evidence.finding: 24-week CT fusion 84% vs 65% autograft; mean time to fusion 14.3 vs 19.7 weeks; two harvest-site infections in controls.

evidence.title: Pivotal trial of Augment Injectable Bone Graft vs autologous bone graft in hindfoot fusions
evidence.finding: Completed April 2013 at 25 sites; supported the 2018 PMA supplement.

evidence.title: Post-approval trial of Augment Injectable vs autologous bone graft in foot and ankle fusions
evidence.finding: Post-approval study; status unknown, no results posted.

bd.reimbursement: Covered by the same C1734 pass-through category as Augment Bone Graft from 2020-01-01 in HOPD and ASC; now packaged. Inpatient bundled in MS-DRG.
bd.notes: Injectable form was built for percutaneous and arthroscopic fusions and ASC workflow; 1.5 cc and 3.0 cc kits.

catalog_status_2026: Stryker's US trauma-and-extremities bone grafting catalog page (read 2026-10-22) lists AlloFiber, AlloMatrix, Augment, BIO4, DBM, FusionFlex, HydroSet XT, Ignite, OsteoSet, Pro-Dense, Pro-Dense LoVisc, Pro-Stim, Tensix, Vitoss, Vitoss BA, Vitoss BA2X and Vitoss BBTrauma as current products.

name: GEM 21S Growth-factor Enhanced Matrix (rhPDGF-BB with beta-TCP)
ownership_history: Developed by BioMimetic Pharmaceuticals (Samuel Lynch); PMA held by Lynch Biologics, LLC since approval; the orthopedic sibling Augment (rhPDGF-BB) went BioMimetic to Wright Medical (2013) to Stryker (2020). GEM 21S was marketed in dentistry by Osteohealth (a Luitpold Pharmaceuticals unit, which also packaged the kit) and Luitpold's Shirley, NY plant manufactured the rhPDGF syringe; current distributor not verified.
composition: 0.3 mg/mL recombinant human PDGF-BB (0.5 mL syringe) mixed chairside with 0.5 cc beta-tricalcium phosphate particles

regulatory.reference: P040013 approved 2005-11-18; supplements through S032 (2024-11-22)
on_label_indications: Treatment of periodontally related defects: intrabony periodontal defects, furcation periodontal defects, and gingival recession associated with periodontal defects

applications.evidence_summary: Pivotal 11-center RCT (Nevins 2005, n=180, intrabony defects of 4 mm or more): rhPDGF-BB with beta-TCP accelerated clinical attachment gain and increased linear bone fill at six months versus beta-TCP alone.
applications.caveats: Sponsor-run; six-month surrogate endpoints; a 2019 meta-analysis found rhPDGF gains comparable to conventional grafting.

applications.evidence_summary: Off-label in sinus lifts and ridge augmentation; the 2013 systematic review found no evidence to support rhPDGF in sinus lift, socket healing or ridge augmentation.
applications.caveats: Off-label.

applications.evidence_summary: Three-patient pilot of cultured marrow MSCs on biphasic scaffold with PDGF in alveolar clefts gave 51 percent fill at three months (2011).
applications.caveats: Off-label, cell-plus-growth-factor construct.

evidence.title: Platelet-derived growth factor stimulates bone fill and rate of attachment level gain: results of a large multicenter randomized controlled trial
evidence.finding: rhPDGF-BB with beta-TCP produced faster clinical attachment gain and more linear bone fill at six months than beta-TCP alone in advanced intrabony defects.

evidence.title: Clinical efficacy of growth factors to enhance tissue repair in oral and maxillofacial reconstruction: systematic review
evidence.finding: rhPDGF-BB reliably increases linear bone fill in intrabony pockets with weaker evidence for lasting attachment gains; no evidence for recession, sinus lift, socket or ridge augmentation; rhBMP-2 effective in sockets and sinus lifts; no controlled data for mandibular segmental repair.

evidence.title: Repair of alveolar cleft defect with mesenchymal stem cells and platelet derived growth factors: preliminary report
evidence.finding: Mean 51.3 percent defect fill at three months in four alveolar clefts treated with cultured marrow MSCs on biphasic scaffold plus rhPDGF.

bd.reimbursement: Periodontal regeneration is CDT D4263 and D4265; private pay or dental plan; no medical code.
bd.notes: The only rhPDGF product in dentistry; low visibility, no new indication since 2005; post-approval study protocols approved 2008 and 2015.

name: Arthrex DX Reinforcement Matrix
ownership_history: Manufactured for Arthrex by DSM Biomedical, Inc. (FDA GUDID record). The sweep brief grouped this with LifeNet allografts; it is a xenograft (not LifeNet) - corrected here.
composition: Decellularized porcine dermal collagen matrix (Arthrex describes a xenograft dermal ECM processed with the OPTRIX method, without cross-linking); GUDID lists a collagen orthopaedic tendon-reinforcement mesh.

regulatory.reference: unverified - GUDID lists product codes OWY (collagen mesh, orthopaedic, tendon reinforcement) and FTM; no K number found for 'DX Reinforcement Matrix'. Lineage candidates: Medeor Matrix K103787 (Kensey Nash, 2011-02-07, cited as predicate for Arthrex SpeedFLEX) and MESO Tendon Matrix K133169 (DSM Biomedical, 2013-12-20, OWY)
on_label_indications: Not read. Cleared collagen mesh in this lineage is for reinforcement of soft tissue where weakness exists / tendon repair reinforcement.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product located (PubMed search 2026-10-23); xenograft dermal patches have a mixed class record (see restore-orthobiologic withdrawn SIS patch).
applications.caveats: Product-specific K number and indications unverified.

evidence.title: Acellular Collagen Matrix Patch Augmentation of Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair Reduces Re-Tear Rates: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Control Trials
evidence.finding: Class evidence only (retear 11% vs 34%).

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure.
bd.notes: Private-label xenograft patch; DSM Biomedical (formerly Kensey Nash) supplier relationship.

name: ArthroFlex Acellular Dermal Matrix (and BioWasher)
ownership_history: Processed by LifeNet Health with Matracell decellularization; marketed by Arthrex. Arthrex and LifeNet partnership terms not read.
composition: Human acellular dermal matrix (>=97% DNA removed, Matracell process, room-temperature storage, 3-year shelf life, SAL 10-6), sizes 0.5-3.0 mm thick; BioWasher is a 10 x 14 mm 2 mm washer.

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) - classification inferred from LifeNet protocol wording ('human cellular tissue product'); the brand-level 361 vs 510(k) status was not confirmed (Arthrex's newer SpeedFLEX dermal allograft was cleared via 510(k) K251690)
on_label_indications: LifeNet sheet: ArthroFlex is an acellular dermal matrix used to supplement soft tissue repairs such as the Achilles tendon and rotator cuff; augment rotator cuff, Achilles, biceps, quad and patellar tendon repairs; reinforce peroneal/tibialis and hand/foot flexor/extensor tendons and capsular repairs

challenge: The 361 HCT/P status of dermal-allograft patches is increasingly contested: Arthrex's SpeedFLEX (decellularized human dermis, LifeNet donor tissue) went the 510(k) route in September 2025.

applications.evidence_summary: Gilot 2015 (Arthroscopy, single-center, prospective, blinded, nonrandomized, n=35: 20 ECM-augmented vs 15 controls, large to massive tears, ~25 months): retears 10% vs 26% (P=.0483), ASES 88.9 vs 72.6. The Cleveland Clinic Florida RCT (NCT03551509) terminated at n=9. Class meta-analyses of acellular patches (5 RCTs, 307 patients) show retear 11% vs 34%.
applications.caveats: Product-specific evidence is one small nonrandomized study; the RCT was terminated; class meta-analyses include other matrices.

applications.evidence_summary: Label covers Achilles, biceps, quad, patellar and hand/foot tendon reinforcement; case reports and technique papers only (e.g., AC joint resurfacing, pectoralis major reconstruction). No comparative study located.
applications.caveats: Expert opinion/case reports only.

evidence.title: Outcome of Large to Massive Rotator Cuff Tears Repaired With and Without Extracellular Matrix Augmentation: A Prospective Comparative Study
evidence.finding: Retears 10% (2/20) with ECM graft vs 26% (4/15) without (P=.0483); pain and ASES better with graft; Level III, nonrandomized.

evidence.title: LifeNet: Extracellular Matrix Graft in Rotator Cuff Repair (RCT, Cleveland Clinic Florida)
evidence.finding: Terminated with 9 patients enrolled (planned 70); results posted.

evidence.title: Acellular Collagen Matrix Patch Augmentation of Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair Reduces Re-Tear Rates: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Control Trials
evidence.finding: Five RCTs: retear 11% with patch vs 34% control (P=.0006); class evidence, not ArthroFlex-specific.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure (OPPS/ASC); tissue cost to facility.
bd.notes: Arthrex sells ArthroFlex (LifeNet-processed allograft), SpeedFLEX (K251690 510(k)) and DX Reinforcement Matrix (xenograft): three patch tiers in one catalog.

name: Collagen Meniscus Implant (CMI; Menaflex; CMI XL)
ownership_history: ReGen Biologics Inc. 510(k) K082079 (ReGen Collagen Scaffold / Menaflex, 2008-12-18) was rescinded by FDA on 2010-10-14, pushing ReGen into bankruptcy; Ivy Sports Medicine (a ReGen investor) kept the product alive and later won on appeal 2-1 against FDA (dates not retrieved). Ivy obtained a new 510(k), K170364 (CMI XL, 2017-05-02). Stryker's Endoscopy division acquired Ivy Sports Medicine on 2016-09-01 (Ry Ortho). Whether Stryker actively markets CMI in the US today is not verified.
composition: Resorbable scaffold of type I collagen from bovine Achilles tendon, semilunar shaped, sutured to the meniscal rim.

regulatory.reference: K170364 Ivy Sports Medicine Collagen Meniscus Implant XL (2017-05-02), product code OLC; prior K082079 (2008-12-18) rescinded 2010
on_label_indications: Intended for use in surgical procedures for the reinforcement and repair of soft tissue injuries of the medial meniscus; the patient must have an intact meniscal rim and anterior and posterior horns for attachment of the mesh, and the surgically prepared site must extend at least into the red-white zone (K170364 and K242302 text)

challenge: The 2008 clearance was rescinded in 2010 (a rare FDA reversal); the 2017 clearance restored a US pathway. The pivotal RCT showed benefit in chronic but not acute patients, and the 20-year follow-up found no chondroprotection.

applications.evidence_summary: Rodkey 2008 (JBJS, RCT, 311 patients across two arms: acute n=157, chronic n=154; mean 59 months): implants produced new meniscus-like tissue and significantly increased meniscal tissue on second look (P=.001); clinical benefit (Lysholm, Tegner, activity) in the chronic group but none in the acute group. 20-year prospective case-control (n=36): no difference vs partial meniscectomy on Lysholm, KOOS, Tegner, IKDC or radiographic OA, so the implant was not chondroprotective. Meta-analysis of CMI vs Actifit (37 studies, 1,276 patients): both improve scores; failure risk 7% CMI vs 9% Actifit.
applications.caveats: ReGen-funded pivotal; most data are medial CMI in selected patients; modest effect, failure risk 7%; long-term chondroprotection not shown.

evidence.title: Comparison of the collagen meniscus implant with partial meniscectomy. A prospective randomized trial
evidence.finding: New meniscus-like tissue formed; chronic-group patients improved clinically with the implant, acute-group patients did not.

evidence.title: Loss of chondroprotection of medial collagen meniscus implant (CMI) at 20-year follow-up
evidence.finding: At about 21 years no clinical or radiographic advantage over partial medial meniscectomy; 1 failure per group.

evidence.title: No differences in clinical outcome between CMI and Actifit meniscal scaffolds: a systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Both scaffolds improved clinical scores; failure risk 7% (CMI) vs 9% (Actifit); evidence quality low.

evidence.title: Clinical outcomes and complications of a collagen meniscus implant: a systematic review
evidence.finding: 11 studies: Lysholm and VAS improved from 6 months to 10 years.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the arthroscopic procedure; coverage often limited by payer policies (not verified).
bd.notes: Stryker holds CMI after buying Ivy in 2016; low-volume niche.

name: FlexBand / FlexBand Plus / FlexPatch (Artelon)
ownership_history: Developed by Artimplant AB (Sweden); assets acquired by International Life Sciences LLC d/b/a Artelon in January 2014 and moved to Marietta, GA; Stryker announced a definitive agreement to acquire Artelon on 2024-06-03 and completed it 2024-07-15 (Business Wire). The 510(k) applicant of record remains International Life Sciences.
composition: Knitted mesh of ARTELON fibers - degradable polycaprolactone-based polyurethane urea (PUUR) - cut to size; FlexBand Plus has pre-loaded suture ends.

regulatory.reference: K192112 FlexBand/FlexBand Plus (2019-09-27); K230316 FlexBand, FlexPatch, FlexBand Plus (2023-05-26); K260317 Artelon Convenience Kits (2026-04-09). Product codes FTL/OWW; Class II surgical mesh
on_label_indications: Reinforcement of soft tissue where weakness exists; reinforcement of tissues repaired by suture or other fixation devices during tendon and ligament repair including rotator cuff, patellar, Achilles, biceps, quadriceps tendons, medial and lateral collateral ligament, spring ligament, deltoid ligament, ulnar collateral ligament or other tendons or extra-articular ligaments (K230316)
Not intended to replace normal body structure or provide the full mechanical strength to support the repaired tissue

applications.evidence_summary: Kelly 2024 (Foot Ankle Spec, retrospective, n=105, mean >6 months, spring ligament, Achilles and Brostrom repairs): 12 complications, 4 major, 1 matrix removal; authors conclude low complication rates. Also technique reports in revision ACL (2026). No comparative study of tendon healing located.
applications.caveats: Retrospective safety series; Stryker/Artelon relationship of authors not read; no efficacy comparison.

applications.evidence_summary: Cleared for rotator cuff reinforcement but no published study of FlexBand in rotator cuff repair located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Label only.

evidence.title: Safety Profile of Synthetic Elastic Degradable Matrix for Soft Tissue Reconstruction in Foot & Ankle Surgery
evidence.finding: 12 complications (4 major); one PUUR matrix removed; safe in foot and ankle soft tissue reconstruction.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure.
bd.notes: Stryker bought Artelon (foot and ankle, sports medicine soft tissue fixation) in July 2024; terms undisclosed.

name: GraftJacket Regenerative Tissue Matrix (incl. GraftJacket Now Ultra-Thick)
ownership_history: Originated at LifeCell (acellular human dermis); marketed for orthopaedic/sports use by Wright Medical Technology (which licensed the GRAFTJACKET brand to KCI for wound care); Stryker acquired Wright Medical in November 2020 (existing atlas record on OsteoSet). Current orthopaedic GraftJacket pages are Stryker-branded and cite AlloSource white papers; a search summary said the sheet lists AlloSource as manufacturer, but the Stryker page read did not name the processor. The brief's LifeCell/AbbVie Allergan processor claim could not be confirmed and may be outdated.
composition: Pre-hydrated acellular human dermal matrix, 3-4 mm 'Ultra-Thick' sizes 4x4, 4x8, 5x7 cm; collagen-rich scaffold retaining growth factors (bFGF, PDGF-bb, TGF-beta, BMP2 per Stryker page, citing AlloSource papers).

regulatory.reference: none (361 HCT/P; establishment registered with CBER) - not stated on the Stryker page read; the existing atlas dermal-allograft record carries the same open question
on_label_indications: Stryker page: used for 'reinforcement, support and protection of soft tissue'; the page does not mention rotator cuff

challenge: Orthopaedic dermal allografts are marketed as 361 HCT/Ps for 'supplemental support', while the evidence is about rotator cuff retear reduction; Arthrex's 2025 SpeedFLEX shows a 510(k) path exists for the same tissue.

applications.evidence_summary: Barber 2012 (Arthroscopy; multicenter prospective randomized, n=42; >3 cm two-tendon tears, single-row repair with GraftJacket vs without, mean 24 months): ASES 98.9 vs 94.8 (P=.035), Constant 91.9 vs 85.3 (P=.008), gadolinium MRI intact cuff 85% vs 40% (P<.01); no graft-related adverse events. Class meta-analyses of matrix augmentation show lower retear.
applications.caveats: The RCT is small and labeled 'lesser quality' (Level II); sponsor/funding not read; an Oxford biopsy series (Rashid 2020, GraftJacket n=4, Permacol n=3) found disrupted native tendon ECM and no cellular benefit at 4 weeks.

applications.evidence_summary: Case-level use for Achilles, biceps and latissimus transfer augmentation (e.g., 2017 case report of latissimus transfer with GraftJacket); no comparative study located.
applications.caveats: Case reports.

evidence.title: A prospective, randomized evaluation of acellular human dermal matrix augmentation for arthroscopic rotator cuff repair
evidence.finding: Augmented repairs had better ASES (98.9 vs 94.8) and Constant scores and 85% vs 40% intact cuffs on MRI at mean 24 months.

evidence.title: Rotator cuff repair with biological graft augmentation causes adverse tissue outcomes
evidence.finding: Biopsies 4 weeks after repair with GraftJacket (n=4), Permacol (n=3) or no patch (n=3) showed native tendon ECM disruption under patches and no increase in cellularity; one adverse immune response with Permacol.

evidence.title: Rotator Cuff Matrix Augmentation and Interposition: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Graft augmentation lowered retear rates (P=.05) and improved ASES vs repair alone; no graft superior to another.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure (OPPS/ASC); tissue cost to facility.
bd.notes: Stryker sells GraftJacket alongside Artelon (2024) and AlloSource-processed cartilage and other grafts; wound-care GraftJacket rights sit with KCI/3M heritage (not read).

name: LARS synthetic ligament (Ligament Advanced Reinforcement System); LARS AC Band / ACJ
ownership_history: LARS device family; the 510(k) applicant was Corin USA for the LARS AC Band (K190143, 2019-11-04) and Movmedix S.A.S. for LARS ACJ (K253115, 2026-06-10). Corporate relationships among LARS SA, Corin and Movmedix not verified. The sweep brief said 'Xiros LARS'; Xiros (Poly-Tape) is a separate company.
composition: Permanent polyethylene terephthalate (polyester) fiber ligament with free intra-articular fibers and woven extra-articular segments (general description); the AC Band is a polyester tissue reinforcement band.

regulatory.reference: K190143 LARS AC Band Device (acromioclavicular fixation, 21 CFR 888.3030, product codes HTN/MBI); K253115 LARS ACJ (2026-06-10). No FDA clearance for LARS as an ACL/PCL graft was found in openFDA (2026-10-23)
on_label_indications: LARS ACJ / AC Band: indicated to provide fixation during the healing process following a syndesmotic trauma, such as fixation of acromioclavicular separations due to coracoclavicular ligament disruptions (K253115 comparison table)

challenge: US clearance covers acromioclavicular fixation only; ACL/PCL reconstruction with LARS is ex-US/off-label. The literature on LARS ACL is mostly from outside the US, with one 55-patient cohort showing a 33% mechanical failure rate at about 8 years.

applications.evidence_summary: LARS for primary ACL reconstruction: single-surgeon cohort of 55 at median 7.8 years had 33.3% mechanical failure (17/51) and 39% secondary procedures; authors say LARS should not be a primary ACL graft option (KSSTA 2019, Level III). Contrasting 2024 retrospective series (n=53, over 35 years) reported 3.8% failure, Lysholm 90.6, but 40% did not return to pre-injury activity. PCL meta-analysis (2022) considers it effective and comparable to hamstring autograft (limited evidence).
applications.caveats: Heterogeneous retrospective series; non-US mostly; US label is AC joint only, so these uses are not authorized.

evidence.title: Primary ACL reconstruction using the LARS device is associated with a high failure rate at minimum of 6-year follow-up
evidence.finding: Mechanical failure 33.3% (17/51) at median 7.8 years; 39.2% secondary operations.

evidence.title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction with LARS Synthetic Ligament: Outcomes and Failures
evidence.finding: Lysholm 90.6, IKDC 80.3, failure 3.8% in patients over 35; about 40% did not return to pre-injury activity.

evidence.title: Ligament Advanced Reinforcement System (LARS) synthetic graft for PCL reconstruction: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: LARS for primary isolated PCL reconstruction seems effective and safe, comparable to 4-strand hamstring autograft; evidence limited.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure.
bd.notes: US presence limited to AC joint clearances; K253115 (2026) shows ongoing US filings.

name: TenoGlide Tendon Protector Sheet (cleared as Tendon Wrap Tendon Protector)
ownership_history: Integra LifeSciences Corporation (Plainsboro, NJ). Integra announced TenoGlide 510(k) clearance and US launch in February 2007 (trade release); whether Integra still sells it was not verified.
composition: Absorbable porous matrix of cross-linked bovine type I collagen and glycosaminoglycan (GAG), a non-constricting protective sheet around injured tendons.

regulatory.reference: K053655 'Tendon Wrap Tendon Protector' (2006-02-03), product code FTM; mapping to the TenoGlide brand is inferred from the 2007 launch release and the identical composition - not stated in the summary read
on_label_indications: Indicated for the management and protection of tendon injuries in which there has been no substantial loss of tendon tissue (K053655 summary)

applications.evidence_summary: 510(k) rested on physician experience, animal testing, biocompatibility and physical testing; the summary says clinical experience 'improves mobility of repaired tendons'. No published human comparative study of TenoGlide located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Label is protect/manage tendon injury; no randomized human data.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure; low-cost sheet.
bd.notes: Cleared predicate for newer tendon protectors (Collagen Matrix wrap K080452 cites K053655 as predicate).

name: TenoMend Collagen Tendon Wrap
ownership_history: Collagen Matrix, Inc., now branded Regenity Biosciences. TenoMend is sold through Exactech (an Exactech page limits TenoMend sales to New Zealand); the FDA clearance is under the Collagen Matrix name. Regenity also sells private-label collagen tendon wraps. NeuroMend (nerve wrap; Stryker distribution since 2007) is a nerve product and is not recorded here.
composition: Resorbable type I collagen matrix sheet (non-constricting tendon encasement); when hydrated a conformable, porous collagen sheet.

regulatory.reference: K080452 Collagen Tendon Wrap (2008-05-15); predicates K053655 (Integra Tendon Wrap) and K060952 (Collagen Nerve Wrap)
on_label_indications: Collagen Tendon Wrap is indicated for the management and protection of tendon injuries in which there has been no substantial loss of tendon tissue (K080452)

applications.evidence_summary: 510(k) was cleared on equivalence to Integra's Tendon Wrap; no clinical study of TenoMend located (PubMed search 2026-10-23).
applications.caveats: Mapping between 'TenoMend' brand and K080452 comes from Exactech/search summary; US commercial availability not confirmed.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure.
bd.notes: US availability uncertain; Exactech page lists New Zealand.

name: VersaWrap Tendon Protector / VersaCoat
ownership_history: Alafair Biosciences, Inc.; ownership not verified further.
composition: Bioresorbable clear hydrogel sheet of alginate and hyaluronic acid with a wetting solution, placed under, around or over injured tissue as a non-constricting interface (K240817).

regulatory.reference: K160364 VersaWrap Tendon Protector (2016-06-10); K200311 (2020-03-06); K240817 VersaWrap (2024-06-14); K251655 VersaCoat Tendon Protector (2025-07-18). Product codes OWW/FTM
on_label_indications: Indicated for the management and protection of tendon injuries in which there has been no substantial loss of tendon tissue; may also be used in the management and protection of surrounding tissues such as skeletal muscle and ligaments (K240817)

applications.evidence_summary: Adu 2024 (Front Surg; Texas Tech hand surgery, retrospective, n=90 tendon repairs and tenolysis, mean follow-up 4.6 months): 92.3% good or excellent function (Strickland), active ROM 88.8%; no comparator. A University of Florida randomized zone 2 flexor tendon trial (NCT04322370, n=11) completed; a 400-patient Achilles trial (NCT07025252) is enrolling by invitation.
applications.caveats: Uncontrolled hand-surgery series; short follow-up; Alafair provided product to a preclinical comparison study (PMID 39306773, results not read).

evidence.title: Evaluating the effect of VersaWrap tendon protector on functional outcomes in operative tendon repairs
evidence.finding: 92.3% good or excellent function at mean 4.6 months; mean ROM 88.8% active.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Commercially Available Antiadhesion Tendon Protector Sheets in Tendon Repair Surgery Versus Tendon Repair Surgery Alone: A Preclinical Model Study
evidence.finding: Preclinical comparison of antiadhesion sheets (VersaWrap supplied by Alafair); results not read.

evidence.title: Prospective randomized blinded trial of VersaWrap Tendon Protector for zone 2 flexor tendon injuries (University of Florida)
evidence.finding: Completed; no results located.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged in the procedure.
bd.notes: Hydrogel antiadhesion sheet used in hand, Achilles, spine; K251655 VersaCoat adds a new brand.

name: Acellular human dermal allograft patches for rotator cuff augmentation (GraftJacket, ArthroFlex, others)
company: GraftJacket: LifeCell/Allergan-processed, marketed by Wright Medical, now Stryker (orthopaedic rights; unverified); ArthroFlex: LifeNet Health, distributed by Arthrex
ownership_history: GraftJacket (Wright Medical, 2002 onward) moved to Stryker with the 2020 Wright acquisition; ArthroFlex launched by Arthrex/LifeNet around 2011 (dates from memory, unverified).
composition: Decellularized human dermis, 1-2 mm thick, sutured over or bridging the repaired cuff; regulated as a 361 HCT/P (no openFDA 510(k) record found for either brand).

regulatory.reference: No premarket number
on_label_indications: none; 361 tissue used at surgeon discretion for tendon augmentation or superior capsular reconstruction

applications.evidence_summary: Multicenter RCT of 42 patients with 2-tendon tears >3 cm: GraftJacket augmentation improved ASES (98.9 vs 94.8) and Constant (91.9 vs 85.3) scores at 24 months with better MRI intact-repair rates (Barber 2012, PMID:21978432). Arthrex is running a 120-patient randomized post-market study of dermal allograft augmentation in large/massive tears (NCT05981833, 2023-2025, status unknown).
applications.caveats: Single small RCT, industry-supported; most other data are superior capsular reconstruction series rather than augmentation.

evidence.title: A prospective, randomized evaluation of acellular human dermal matrix augmentation for arthroscopic rotator cuff repair
evidence.finding: Statistically better ASES and Constant scores with augmentation at mean 24 months.

evidence.title: Randomized post-market study evaluating dermal allograft augmentation of large and massive rotator cuff tears
evidence.finding: Arthrex-sponsored; primary completion September 2025; status unknown.

bd.reimbursement: Packaged into the ASC/HOPD procedure payment; in HOPD the tissue may be reported with HCPCS C1762 (connective tissue, human) but it is packaged, not separately paid.
bd.notes: Tissue-bank margin flows to the distributor (Arthrex, Stryker); the same reps sell anchors and the bone biologics in the atlas.

challenge: Tried Stryker's US GraftJacket and trauma-and-extremities pages (404) and openFDA (no GraftJacket 510(k) under the GRAFTJACKET or LIFECELL names); no primary source stating the regulatory status or the current Stryker/LifeCell/Allergan rights was retrieved. 361 status is the working assumption.

name: CornerLoc SI Joint Fusion grafts
composition: Two machined cortical bone allografts placed orthogonally into the prepared posterior joint through two small incisions, with a demineralized bone matrix sponge; non-transfixing. The company's TransLoc 3D (K232878, Oct 2023) is a 3D-printed titanium modular posterior implant plus lateral-oblique screws (hybrid) and is a device.

on_label_indications: Homologous use: structural allograft bone placed in the sacroiliac joint (HCT/P, no FDA-cleared indication)

applications.evidence_summary: No peer-reviewed clinical series of the allograft retrieved; physician and hospital pages (UK HealthCare) describe the technique and a 12-month ossification timeline. CornerLoc's registered studies (NCT05916092 SPARTAN n=240; NCT06487936 registry) cover the titanium TransLoc 3D.
applications.caveats: Company founded 2017 (Tulsa, OK); evidence for the graft product is descriptive only; the hybrid TransLoc 3D exists because the posterior allograft alone is non-covered under the 2025 LCDs.

evidence.title: SPARTAN: post-market study of TransLoc 3D screw-only vs hybrid constructs
evidence.finding: Company reports 91.7% improved in pain and function at 6 months (interim, unpublished).

bd.reimbursement: CPT 27278 (intra-articular, no cortical piercing) unless a cortical-piercing variant or hybrid (27279); ASC device-intensive 2026; non-covered by CGS/Noridian/Palmetto LCDs (transfixation required); implant packaged, no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: Private; sells surgery-ready trays to pain practices and ASCs. The DBM sponge is unbranded in all sources.

challenge: Tissue bank and the DBM brand are not disclosed; launch year inferred from the 2017 founding and 2018-2019 physician adoption, not a dated release.

name: Cortical strut / fibular strut allograft (structural allograft)
company: Tissue banks (MTF Biologics, AlloSource, LifeNet Health, RTI/Surgalign heritage) and distributing implant companies
composition: Freeze-dried or fresh-frozen human cortical bone (fibular shaft segments, femoral or tibial cortical struts), sometimes machined; minimally manipulated, homologous use.

regulatory.reference: Regulated solely under section 361 of the PHS Act and 21 CFR 1271 (establishment registration, no premarket review)
on_label_indications: Not labeled with indications; HCT/P for homologous structural use as determined by the surgeon

applications.evidence_summary: Haddad/Duncan 2002 multicenter series: 39 of 40 Vancouver B1 fractures united with cortical onlay strut allografts alone (19) or with a plate (21), with increased bone stock. A later pooled review of locking-plate fixation (135 fractures, 91% union) and a 20-patient series without struts (18 of 19 healed) show modern plates reduce but do not eliminate the role of struts, which are reserved for poor bone stock and medial comminution.
applications.caveats: Retrospective; allograft resorption and stress shielding over the long term not addressed.

applications.evidence_summary: Non-vascularized fibular (auto- or allo-) graft across the neck with revision fixation is reported in small series, mostly from India and China; vascularized fibular autograft series report union in all patients (n=13, n=29).
applications.caveats: Small series; the US standard for young patients is valgus osteotomy.

applications.evidence_summary: Free vascularized fibular autograft (Urbaniak) is the structural benchmark for pre-collapse lesions; non-vascularized fibular allograft is a lower-morbidity alternative. A 2023 network meta-analysis of 18 RCTs ranked free fibula and vascularized bone grafting above core decompression alone for preventing progression.
applications.caveats: Autograft, not allograft, in most RCTs; technically demanding.

applications.evidence_summary: Best-supported augmentation in upper-extremity trauma: meta-analysis of 10 studies (n=802) found fibular allograft with a locking plate preserved humeral head height (WMD -2.40 mm) and neck-shaft angle (WMD -5.71 degrees), improved ASES (+5.08) and cut major complications (OR 0.37) with no difference in revision (Dasari 2022, PMID:34906682). A 2026 meta-analysis restricted to 5 RCTs (n=350) found graft augmentation lowered complications (OR 0.21) and biologic grafts shortened healing by 3.25 weeks (Daher 2026, PMID:42750779). Cadaver loading: 0 of 8 augmented vs 6 of 8 unaugmented constructs collapsed (PMID:21782474).
applications.caveats: Mostly retrospective comparisons and Chinese single-center RCTs; graft fate (incorporation vs resorption) and long-term outcomes undefined (PMID:32030961); a new RCT uses femoral head allograft instead (NCT07538700, 2025-2029). No proof that augmentation beats reverse arthroplasty in the 75+ group where ORIF volume is falling.

evidence.title: Periprosthetic femoral fractures around well-fixed implants: use of cortical onlay allografts with or without a plate.
evidence.finding: 98% union with strut allografts with or without a plate; struts act as biological plates and add bone stock.

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of surgical interventions for osteonecrosis of the femoral head: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
evidence.finding: Across 18 RCTs, autologous bone grafting plus BMAC, free fibula, vascularized bone graft and biomaterial plus vascularized graft all delayed progression versus core decompression alone; no difference in THA conversion.

evidence.title: Free vascularised fibular graft for neglected femoral neck fractures in young adults.
evidence.finding: All 13 neglected femoral neck fractures united at a mean 4.8 months; coxa vara common.

evidence.title: Improved outcomes for proximal humerus fracture ORIF augmented with a fibular allograft in elderly patients: systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Better radiographic maintenance, ASES and fewer major complications with fibular allograft; no revision difference.

evidence.title: Bone graft augmentation reduces complications in osteosynthesis of proximal humerus fractures: meta-analysis of RCTs
evidence.finding: Five RCTs; OR 0.21 for complications; biologic grafts healed 3.25 weeks faster with less pain.

evidence.title: Indirect medial reduction and strut support of proximal humerus fractures using an endosteal implant
evidence.finding: Technique description of the endosteal fibular allograft incorporated into the locking construct.

evidence.title: Proximal humeral fracture fixation: locking plate construct with or without intramedullary fibular allograft
evidence.finding: No augmented construct collapsed under 25,000 cycles vs 6 of 8 unaugmented.

evidence.title: Hip-allograft in proximal humerus fractures versus plate implantation alone: RCT
evidence.finding: Recruiting (Netherlands); femoral head allograft vs plate alone; primary completion May 2029.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in inpatient MS-DRG (revision THA or periprosthetic fracture DRGs); allograft cost is a hospital supply expense.
bd.notes: Commodity-priced, tissue-bank supplied, usually contracted through the hospital's tissue services agreement rather than the implant contract; implant companies co-market struts with cable-plate systems.

ownership_history: Not a branded product; cortical fibula segments are standard tissue-bank inventory. The endosteal technique was described by Gardner, Helfet and Lorich at HSS (Gardner 2008, PMID:18317054).

name: Fresh distal tibia allograft (DTA) for glenoid reconstruction
company: Tissue banks supplying fresh osteochondral grafts (JRF Ortho, MTF Biologics); technique popularized by Provencher
ownership_history: Not branded; fresh (non-frozen) lateral distal tibia plafond segments are allocated by tissue banks with a short shelf life.
composition: Fresh osteochondral lateral distal tibia, cut to match the anterior glenoid defect and fixed with two screws or suture buttons.

regulatory.reference: No premarket number; fresh osteochondral allograft under 21 CFR 1271
on_label_indications: none

applications.evidence_summary: Matched cohort of 50 DTA vs 50 Latarjet with at least 15% bone loss: equivalent ASES, WOSI and SANE at 45 months despite larger defects in the DTA group (Frank 2018, PMID:29389219). DTA case series: 89% graft healing on CT, 3% lysis, no recurrence in 27 patients (Provencher 2017, PMID:28017469). Systematic review of allograft glenoid reconstruction (283 shoulders): recurrence 3.9%, healing 93.5% (Villatte 2020, PMID:32524228). First RCT vs Latarjet recruiting (NCT05658289, n=68).
applications.caveats: Retrospective and single-surgeon data; fresh graft logistics and cost; resorption concerns after arthroscopic DTA (Wong 2018, PMID:30095986).

evidence.title: Outcomes of Latarjet versus distal tibia allograft for anterior shoulder instability repair: a matched cohort analysis
evidence.finding: No significant difference in postoperative scores between Latarjet and DTA.

evidence.title: Distal tibia allograft glenoid reconstruction in recurrent anterior shoulder instability: clinical and radiographic outcomes
evidence.finding: ASES 63 to 91; 89% allograft healing; no recurrent instability at 45 months.

evidence.title: Use of allograft to reconstruct anterior bony glenoid defect in chronic glenohumeral instability: a systematic review
evidence.finding: Recurrence 3.9%, allograft healing 93.5% across 10 studies.

evidence.title: Latarjet vs anatomic glenoid reconstruction (DTA with Bankart repair): prospective multicentre RCT
evidence.finding: Recruiting; primary completion January 2026.

bd.reimbursement: Shoulder stabilization with bone block is an outpatient/ASC procedure; the fresh graft is packaged into the facility payment (in HOPD it may be reported with the connective-tissue HCPCS C1762 but is still packaged). The graft's price (thousands of dollars) is the commercial obstacle vs a free coracoid.
bd.notes: Sports-medicine reps (Arthrex, Smith+Nephew, Stryker, DePuy Mitek) sell the fixation and the instruments; the tissue bank sells the graft. A BD role here is about tissue-bank partnerships, not a device.

name: LinQ SI Joint Stabilization System (and TRAQ)
composition: Machined structural cortical bone allograft ('almond-shaped' with a graft window), placed posteriorly into the decorticated mid-joint; TRAQ (2026) is a cortical-piercing allograft variant engaging sacral and iliac cortices at four points. Window may be packed with DBM at surgeon discretion (physician descriptions; not in the IFU text retrieved).

on_label_indications: Homologous use: structural allograft bone placed in the sacroiliac joint (HCT/P, no FDA-cleared indication)

applications.evidence_summary: SECURE (NCT04423120; Calodney 2024, PMID 38524688): prospective single-arm, 16 US sites, 122 implanted, composite responder 73.5% at 12 months, one procedure-related SAE; no CT fusion endpoint. Bovinet 2025 (PMID 40832586): retrospective 6-site cohort n=258, NRS 7.6 to 1.6 at mean 1.75 years. Ampomah 2025 (PMID 40828365): n=260, AE 1.9% at 6 months. LINQT RCT vs conservative management (NCT07558278, n=200, started Jul 2026) is the first randomized trial of any posterior allograft.
applications.caveats: All clinical data are pain/function case series by interventional pain physicians with company involvement; no radiographic fusion rate; no comparison to lateral transfixing implants; three MAC LCDs (2025) non-cover procedures without a transfixation device.

evidence.title: SECURE: single-arm multicenter prospective study of LinQ
evidence.finding: 73.5% composite responders at 12 months; one procedure-related serious AE.

evidence.title: Safety, efficacy and durability of outcomes: results from SECURE
evidence.finding: VAS and ODI significantly improved at 12 months; responder rate stable 66-74% across visits.

evidence.title: Minimally invasive posterior SI joint fusion with a novel cortical allograft: real-world long-term outcomes, multisite US cohort
evidence.finding: Mean NRS reduction 6.0 points at 91 weeks; no serious AEs reported.

evidence.title: Retrospective evaluation of adverse events in posterior approach with bone allograft
evidence.finding: AE incidence 2.3% at 3 months and 1.9% at 6 months; no device-related events.

evidence.title: Multicenter retrospective analysis of a posterior sacroiliac fusion device (LinQ)
evidence.finding: NRS 6.98 to 3.06 at mean 612 days; no major AEs.

evidence.title: LINQT: open-label RCT of LinQ vs conventional medical management
evidence.finding: Enrolling; primary endpoint composite responder at 6 months, follow-up 24 months.

evidence.title: TRAQTION: post-market single-arm study of TRAQ
evidence.finding: Enrolling; 24-month follow-up.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 27278 (intra-articular, no cortical piercing) unless a cortical-piercing variant or hybrid (27279); ASC device-intensive 2026; non-covered by CGS/Noridian/Palmetto LCDs (transfixation required); implant packaged, no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: PainTEQ's clinician page states LinQ and TRAQ are HCT/Ps 'regulated solely under Section 361' and 'not FDA-cleared or FDA-approved medical devices'. PainTEQ drove the 0775T (2022) and 27278 (2024) code applications using SECURE interim data. Company ranked on Inc. 5000 (2024). Office-based-lab 27278 physician payment ($13,834 in 2026) is the economic engine for interventional pain practices.

ownership_history: PainTEQ (Tampa, FL) private; majority growth recapitalization co-led by Signet Healthcare Partners and Windham Capital Partners, Aug 2025.
challenge: Tissue bank that processes LinQ not disclosed in any public source retrieved; 'DBM packed in the window' comes from physician/trade descriptions, not the IFU.

name: PsiF Posterior SI Fusion allograft
composition: Structural allograft bone implant placed through a postero-inferior intra-articular trajectory into a decorticated channel in the articular joint, secured mortise-and-tenon in subchondral bone (Lynch 2022). PsiF DNA (510(k) May 2025, launched Jan 2026) is a titanium double-helix transfixing implant placed ilium-to-sacrum that is packed with graft and leverages self-harvested autograft; PsiFGuard (SpineGuard, K-cleared Oct 2024) is the drilling-guidance device.

on_label_indications: Homologous use: structural allograft bone placed in the sacroiliac joint (HCT/P, no FDA-cleared indication)

applications.evidence_summary: Lynch 2022 (PMID 36420375): 57-patient multicenter registry, back pain 6.8 to 3.8 at 6 months. Kaye 2024 (PMID 39087970): LSU Shreveport single-center series of 72 posterior fusions (83% LinQ, remainder PsiF), VAS -3.6 cm, no procedure-related AEs, 54% with one-year follow-up. Latif 2023 (PMID 37511749) is a technique paper for PsiF DNA.
applications.caveats: Small registries with company-affiliated authors; PsiF results are pooled with LinQ in the only independent series; no fusion imaging endpoint.

evidence.title: Minimally invasive inferior intra-articular SI joint fusion with allograft bone
evidence.finding: Back pain 6.8 to 3.8 at 6 months; all outcomes p<0.001; no fusion endpoint.

evidence.title: Posterior sacroiliac fusion surgery: retrospective single-center study (LinQ and PsiF)
evidence.finding: VAS -3.6 cm from 9.5; 38.5% with >=50% improvement; zero procedure-related AEs; 26% withdrawal.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 27278 (intra-articular, no cortical piercing) unless a cortical-piercing variant or hybrid (27279); ASC device-intensive 2026; non-covered by CGS/Noridian/Palmetto LCDs (transfixation required); implant packaged, no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: Omnia Medical (Morgantown, WV), private. The shift from the PsiF allograft to the 510(k) titanium PsiF DNA (transfixing, 27279-eligible) is the clearest example of a posterior vendor re-engineering around the 2025 LCDs.

challenge: Omnia's site does not describe the original PsiF implant's material; its allograft nature is taken from Kaye 2024 ('sacroiliac fusion allograft implants ... PsiF System from Omnia Medical') and Lynch 2022. Tissue bank and launch year not disclosed.

name: SiLO Posterior SI-Fusion System (allograft)
composition: Single dowel of human cortical bone with three circumferential ridges ('Dowel Anchorage Design') and dual vertical side channels that accept additional bone graft during insertion; posterior intra-articular, non-transfixing. SiLO TFX (K221047, Oct 2022; titanium cone plus ilium and sacrum screws, graft placed in the barrel) is the company's 510(k) transfixing hybrid and is a device, not a biologic.

on_label_indications: Homologous use: structural allograft bone placed in the sacroiliac joint (HCT/P, no FDA-cleared indication)

applications.evidence_summary: No peer-reviewed clinical series for the SiLO allograft was retrieved; the company reported >2,500 SiLO procedures in the US (June 2025 release) and a cadaveric study of SiLO TFX. Aurora launched 'Aurora Biologics' in late 2025 to sell biologics with its implants.
applications.caveats: Company-reported volume only; SiLO TFX revenue grew 135% in 2024 and aggregate SI implant sales +8.4% in 2025 (press releases), implying the titanium hybrid, not the allograft, is the growth product after the 2025 LCDs.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 27278 (intra-articular, no cortical piercing) unless a cortical-piercing variant or hybrid (27279); ASC device-intensive 2026; non-covered by CGS/Noridian/Palmetto LCDs (transfixation required); implant packaged, no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: Aurora Spine (TSXV: ASG / OTC: ASAPF), FY2025 revenue $18.4M (+4.6%); SI implants are one of three product lines. Distributor-based sales.

challenge: Tissue processor not disclosed; no clinical outcomes paper found for the allograft; SiLO vs SiLO TFX volumes not separated.

name: Structural allograft (femoral head, bulk tricortical and shaped allograft wedges)
company: Tissue banks (MTF Biologics, AlloSource, LifeNet Health, RTI/Surgalign successors) and hardware companies that private-label allograft wedges
ownership_history: Not applicable.
composition: Fresh-frozen or freeze-dried human femoral head or cortical-cancellous block, shaped intraoperatively or supplied as preformed wedges (Cotton, Evans, interposition)

regulatory.reference: none
on_label_indications: Homologous use as structural bone graft; no FDA-reviewed indication

applications.evidence_summary: Cifaldi 2022 (PMID 35585002): systematic review of 11 studies, 175 patients with TTC arthrodesis and structural allograft (mostly femoral head with a retrograde nail); union 67.4%, limb salvage 92.5%, complications 26.6%, allograft collapse 1.2%. Jeng 2013 (PMID 23650649): 32 patients, 50% radiographic fusion, every diabetic patient a nonunion, 19% below-knee amputation, 71% functional limb salvage counting asymptomatic nonunions.
applications.caveats: High nonunion despite high limb salvage; 3D-printed titanium cages now report 88-89% pooled union (PMID 41724588, PMID 42600975) and one comparative study favored the cage over femoral head for fusion and subsidence.

applications.evidence_summary: Femoral-head and bulk allograft used to restore medial-column length after wedge resection; PMID 34677103 reported high fusion in 14 bone-block TTC fusions with allograft plus BMAC plus DBM and prolonged protected weight-bearing.
applications.caveats: Small series; Charcot subgroup outcomes worse.

applications.evidence_summary: Interposition allograft block for salvage of failed first MTP implant arthroplasty; pooled nonunion 16.5% across 76 patients (PMID 37165627).
applications.caveats: Six level-IV studies.

applications.evidence_summary: Preformed allograft wedges are the most common Cotton and Evans osteotomy spacer; no comparative outcome data found.
applications.caveats: Expert practice.

evidence.title: Tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis with structural allograft for management of large osseous defects of the hindfoot and ankle: a systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Union 67.4%, limb salvage 92.5%; no difference nail vs plate.

evidence.title: Tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis with bulk femoral head allograft for salvage of large defects in the ankle
evidence.finding: 50% fusion; diabetes the only predictor of nonunion; 19% amputation.

evidence.title: Tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis using a novel retrograde intramedullary nail
evidence.finding: 70% fusion overall; 76.5% in the 17 patients needing femoral-head allograft.

evidence.title: Patient-specific 3D-printed porous titanium implants for complex foot and ankle reconstruction: a current concepts review
evidence.finding: Pooled union 89%, limb salvage 92%, reoperation 26%; the single comparative study favored the cage over femoral-head allograft.

bd.reimbursement: No separate payment; bundled or packaged. Allograft is usually procured under the hospital's tissue-bank agreement.
bd.notes: Commodity-priced; the competitive threat is custom 3D-printed titanium (restor3d, 4WEB, Paragon 28/Zimmer Biomet) which carries a much higher ASP and is displacing femoral head in TTC salvage at academic centers.

name: Structural cortical allograft rings and blocks for ACDF (e.g., Cornerstone-SR, AVS/ Bio AVS, MTF and AlloSource cortical rings)
company: Multiple (MTF Biologics, AlloSource, LifeNet Health, RTI/Xtant; branded by Medtronic, Stryker, DePuy Synthes, Globus and others)
ownership_history: Commodity tissue-bank product supplied under private label to most spine companies; Medtronic's Cornerstone-SR ring was the carrier in its cervical rhBMP-2 trials.
composition: Machined cortical (fibula or femoral ring) or corticocancellous allograft spacers with a central window for graft; often paired with a filler (local bone, DBM, i-FACTOR, cellular allograft)

regulatory.reference: Section 361 HCT/P (minimally manipulated structural bone)
on_label_indications: Structural bone graft for cervical interbody fusion (homologous use); PEEK and titanium spacers are devices, not biologics

applications.evidence_summary: Meta-analysis of prospective plated ACDF studies: pseudarthrosis 4.8% with allograft vs 0.9% with autograft (Shriver 2015); 2024 meta-analysis of 34 studies/3,451 segments found structural allograft fusion rates not different from cages at 3-12 months but more hardware complications (Li 2024).
applications.caveats: Comparisons are across studies, not head-to-head RCTs; dysphagia rates do not differ between allograft and autograft (Shriver 2017).

evidence.title: Pseudoarthrosis rates in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: a meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Overall pseudarthrosis 2.6%; autograft 0.9% vs allograft 4.8%.

evidence.title: Fusion rates at different times of cortical iliac crest autograft or allograft compared with cages after ACDF: a meta-analysis
evidence.finding: Structural allograft vs cage: no significant fusion difference at 3, 6 or 12 months; higher hardware complications with allograft.

bd.reimbursement: Inpatient bundled in MS-DRGs 471-473; physician add-on +20931 (structural allograft) is separately reportable and, unlike +20930, is not a Medicare 0-RVU bundled code (confirm current status indicator).
bd.notes: Low-margin commodity; the strategic value is in the filler sold with the ring (i-FACTOR, cellular allografts). MTF, AlloSource and LifeNet all private-label rings for device companies.

name: Vyrsa Pro cortical allograft (Vyrsa V1 titanium is the device)
company: Globus Medical (via Nevro, via Vyrsa Technologies)
composition: Custom cortical allograft implant for posterior SI joint fusion delivered through an 'inferior inlet' approach (Nevro acquisition release, Nov 2023). Vyrsa V1 (introduced end-2022) and Nevro1 (NCT06909292, 'SI transfixing and fusion system') are the titanium transfixing systems in the same portfolio.

on_label_indications: Homologous use: structural allograft bone placed in the sacroiliac joint (HCT/P, no FDA-cleared indication)

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical publication retrieved for Vyrsa Pro. Nevro's post-market study NCT06909292 (n=180, completed May 2025) covers the titanium Nevro1 transfixing system.
applications.caveats: Portfolio changed hands twice in 17 months (Vyrsa -> Nevro, 30 Nov 2023, $40M plus up to $35M milestones; Nevro -> Globus, closed 3 Apr 2025, ~$250M); current Globus branding and catalog status of the allograft not confirmed.

evidence.title: Post-market multicenter study of the Nevro1 SI transfixing and fusion system
evidence.finding: Completed May 2025; results not posted; titanium transfixing device, not the allograft.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 27278 (intra-articular, no cortical piercing) unless a cortical-piercing variant or hybrid (27279); ASC device-intensive 2026; non-covered by CGS/Noridian/Palmetto LCDs (transfixation required); implant packaged, no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: Globus now owns both a lateral HA-coated screw line (SI-LOK/SI-LOK SELECT) and the Vyrsa posterior portfolio; Globus product pages name no graft brand for either, so the Osteocel-with-SI-LOK pairing in the brief is unverified.

ownership_history: Vyrsa Technologies (founded 2021) -> Nevro Corp (30 Nov 2023) -> Globus Medical (3 Apr 2025).
challenge: Vyrsa Pro's current availability under Globus, tissue bank and procedure volumes are not public.

name: iFuse INTRA V and iFuse INTRA X Allograft Implant Systems
composition: INTRA V (formerly INTRA): single triangular cortical allograft; INTRA X: two small cylindrical bone allografts; both 'implantable bone products manufactured from sterilized recovered cadaveric bone tissue', placed intra-articularly through a ~2 cm posterior incision.

on_label_indications: Homologous use: structural allograft bone placed in the sacroiliac joint (HCT/P, no FDA-cleared indication)

applications.evidence_summary: No clinical study retrieved; SI-BONE's product pages cite only finite-element analysis of SI joint motion and state the results are 'not necessarily indicative of human clinical results'. The FY2025 10-K attributes reduced INTRA X demand to the 2024-2025 MAC LCDs precluding coverage of CPT 27278.
applications.caveats: Launched 2024 as a defensive entry into the interventional-pain posterior segment; no SI-BONE-sponsored trial lists the allograft products (NCT07565545 is the titanium INTRA Ti). Manufactured and distributed as HCT/Ps by an undisclosed third-party tissue bank.

evidence.title: iFuse INTRA Ti (titanium posterior-inferior intra-articular cortical-piercing implant) safety and effectiveness
evidence.finding: Not yet recruiting (start Sep 2026); titanium successor billed under 27279, not the allograft.

bd.reimbursement: CPT 27278 (intra-articular, no cortical piercing) unless a cortical-piercing variant or hybrid (27279); ASC device-intensive 2026; non-covered by CGS/Noridian/Palmetto LCDs (transfixation required); implant packaged, no separate HCPCS.
bd.notes: 10-K: 'Our iFuse INTRA/INTRA X implants are derived from human bone tissue ... manufactured and distributed by a third-party as HCT/P products'; 10-K maps INTRA X to CPT 27278 ($441 facility / $13,834 OBL physician fee 2026) and the titanium products to 27279. SI-BONE sells direct (89 territory managers, 83 clinical specialists, 320 agents, FY2025).

challenge: Tissue bank not named; no clinical data; the 2024 launch year comes from the 10-K product chronology, not a dated release.

name: Actifuse (ABX, Flow, Shape, Mis System) silicate-substituted calcium phosphate
ownership_history: Developed by ApaTech (UK); Baxter acquired ApaTech for $330 million in 2010 and continues to list Actifuse and Altapore under Baxter Advanced Surgery (no divestiture found through 2025).
composition: Silicate-substituted calcium phosphate (0.8 wt% silicon in hydroxyapatite), 80% porosity granules; Flow and Shape add a polymer/aqueous carrier

regulatory.reference: K082575 (ApaTech, cleared 2008-11-25; spine including posterolateral fusion with stabilizing hardware); K090850 (dental, 2009); later Baxter clearances for Actifuse Flow/Shape and Altapore (2018)
on_label_indications: Packed gently into bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system including the spine, and in posterolateral fusion procedures with appropriate stabilizing hardware (K082575)

applications.evidence_summary: Small Australian RCT (Licina 2015, n=19): Actifuse 9/9 vs Infuse 8/9 fused at 12 months with similar clinical outcomes.
applications.caveats: n=19, single center; underpowered to show noninferiority.

evidence.title: Comparison of silicate-substituted calcium phosphate (Actifuse) with rhBMP-2 (Infuse) in posterolateral instrumented lumbar fusion
evidence.finding: Fusion 9/9 (SiCaP) vs 8/9 (rhBMP-2); comparable pain and QoL.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in fusion MS-DRGs.
bd.notes: Baxter Advanced Surgery sells direct; Actifuse is a small line inside a large surgical-sealant portfolio and periodically appears on divestiture speculation lists, but no sale was found.

name: Altapore, Altapore Shape and Altapore MIS (SiCaP EP)
ownership_history: ApaTech (UK) originated the silicate-substituted calcium phosphate line; Baxter owns it (Baxter's acquisition of ApaTech not re-sourced). Baxter's current catalog lists Actifuse and Altapore; no divestiture found.
composition: Silicate-substituted calcium phosphate ceramic with enhanced strut porosity (31 to 47%), sold as granules, a shaped strip and a minimally invasive delivery form; sister to Actifuse (which has its own atlas record).

regulatory.reference: K181225 (Altapore, Aug 2018); K192363 (Altapore, Jan 2020, adds posterolateral spine); K191513 and K200640 (Altapore Shape); K201464 (Altapore MIS); K241564 (Actifuse and Altapore combined, Aug 2024)
on_label_indications: Altapore (K192363): implant to fill bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system 'extremities, posterolateral spine and pelvis'; can be used by itself, with autograft as an extender or with bone marrow aspirate; resorbs and is replaced with bone
K241564 adds the intervertebral disc space: must be used with a cage cleared for use with a bone void filler

applications.evidence_summary: SiCaP EP (Altapore) single-arm, open-label multicenter study in instrumented PLF: 102 per-protocol patients, fusion success 86.3% at 12 months and 90.6% at 24 months by CT (PMID 30834972; NCT01452022).
applications.caveats: No autograft control; Baxter authors; fusion success defined by the sponsor protocol.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: Altapore OR SiCaP EP interbody).
applications.caveats: On-label with an interbody device cleared for bone void filler use (K241564); the PLF study did not test interbody use.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: Altapore OR SiCaP tibial plateau).
applications.caveats: Extremities named in the label.

evidence.title: Evaluation of an increased strut porosity silicate-substituted calcium phosphate, SiCaP EP, as a synthetic bone graft substitute in spinal fusion surgery: a prospective, open-label study
evidence.finding: Fusion success was 86.3% (88/102) at month 12 and 90.6% at month 24 with improved pain and function.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in MS-DRG inpatient; packaged in OPPS and ASC payment; no separate HCPCS code or pass-through for bone void fillers.
bd.notes: Baxter sells through its surgical (biosurgery) bone repair catalog.

name: AttraX Putty and AttraX Scaffold
ownership_history: Progentix Orthobiology (Bilthoven, NL) originated AttraX/Curios; NuVasive held the AttraX clearances from 2017 (K172497); Globus Medical completed its NuVasive merger in September 2023 (merger date from public record, not re-sourced).
composition: Synthetic biphasic calcium phosphate ceramic granules with a needle-like surface topography (Progentix/Curios technology): the Putty is ceramic granules premixed with a polymeric binder; the Scaffold is a moldable strip form.

regulatory.reference: K191974 (AttraX Putty, Nov 2019); K240507 (AttraX Scaffold, March 2024); K172497 (Scaffold, 2017); original K151584 (AttraX Putty, Progentix Orthobiology, Oct 2015)
on_label_indications: AttraX Putty (K191974): implant to fill bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system 'posterolateral spine and pelvis', may be used in combination with autogenous bone; resorbs and is replaced with bone

AttraX Scaffold (K240507): posterolateral spine, intervertebral disc space and pelvis; in the posterolateral spine must be used with autogenous bone or bone marrow aspirate; in intervertebral body fusion must be used with a cage cleared for use with a bone void filler
Globus's website also states a Putty interbody indication; the 510(k) supporting it was not located (unverified)

applications.evidence_summary: Dutch multicenter, intrapatient-controlled noninferiority RCT (n=100 enrolled, 87 analysed, 146 instrumented segments): 1-year PLF rate 55% AttraX Putty vs 52% autograft side, difference 2.3% (90% CI -9.1 to 13.7), noninferior (PMID 32080013); at 2 years 70% vs 68%, no difference (PMID 32459724).
applications.caveats: Fusion rates of 52 to 55% at one year are low in absolute terms (CT-based); intrapatient design with local bone in all segments; a published erratum exists (PMID 34183620); conflicts disclosed in the paper were not individually reviewed.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: AttraX Putty interbody OR TLIF OR PLIF).
applications.caveats: On-label only for AttraX Scaffold with an FDA-cleared cage for use with a bone void filler; in the Dutch RCT 62% of patients also had an interbody procedure but the graft under test was posterolateral.

applications.evidence_summary: NuVasive registered a randomized AttraX Putty versus autograft XLIF trial (NCT02250248, n=45, completed May 2021); no peer-reviewed results were located.
applications.caveats: Registry-only evidence; sponsor-run. Putty label (K191974) does not name interbody; the Scaffold label does.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: AttraX pelvis; AttraX acetabular).
applications.caveats: Pelvis is named in both labels; no product-specific pelvic series located.

evidence.title: Efficacy of a Standalone Microporous Ceramic Versus Autograft in Instrumented Posterolateral Spinal Fusion: A Multicenter, Randomized, Intrapatient Controlled, Noninferiority Trial
evidence.finding: AttraX Putty fusion 55% vs autograft 52% at 1 year, noninferior within a 15% margin.

evidence.title: Increasing Fusion Rate Between 1 and 2 Years After Instrumented Posterolateral Spinal Fusion and the Role of Bone Grafting
evidence.finding: Fusion rose to 70% (AttraX Putty) and 68% (autograft) at 2 years with no difference between grafts.

evidence.title: AttraX Putty vs. Autograft in XLIF (NuVasive)
evidence.finding: Registered randomized comparison of AttraX Putty and autograft in lateral interbody fusion; completed, no published results located.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in MS-DRG inpatient; packaged in OPPS and ASC payment; no separate HCPCS code or pass-through for bone void fillers.
bd.notes: Strongest-evidenced synthetic in this slice: only one with a published Level I PLF noninferiority RCT. Globus markets it with its own spine implant franchise.

name: Bi-Ostetic Foam / Putty and Bi-Ostetic Bioactive Glass Foam
ownership_history: Berkeley Advanced Biomaterials (San Leandro, CA) is the 510(k) holder and trademark owner in FDA records; a SeaSpine-branded Bi-Ostetic block appears in a device catalog, distribution relationship not confirmed.
composition: Collagen-ceramic composite: hydroxyapatite and beta-TCP (about 60/40 per catalog listings) with bovine collagen; the Bioactive Glass Foam adds 45S5 bioactive glass particles.

regulatory.reference: K170917 (Bioactive Glass Foam, Oct 2017); K092046 (Foam and Putty, March 2010); K053213 (Foam, 2006); K023703 (Bi-Ostetic, Jan 2003)
on_label_indications: Bi-Ostetic Bioactive Glass Foam (K170917): bony voids or gaps of the skeletal system 'extremities, pelvis and posterolateral spine'; surgically created or traumatic; in the posterolateral spine must be used with autogenous bone marrow aspirate and autograft
Bi-Ostetic Foam/Putty (K092046): extremities, posterolateral spine and pelvis; in weight-bearing situations use with internal or external fixation; treated fracture defect should not exceed 30 mL

applications.evidence_summary: Only an animal study: a 69-rabbit posterolateral fusion model comparing the bioactive glass foam and FormaGraft with iliac crest graft showed comparable healing (PMID 28852357). No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: Bi-Ostetic posterolateral fusion; mineralized collagen bioactive glass spine).
applications.caveats: Preclinical only; label requires bone marrow aspirate plus autograft in the spine.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: Bi-Ostetic tibial plateau; Bi-Ostetic extremities).
applications.caveats: Label caps the treated fracture defect at 30 mL and requires fixation in weight-bearing sites.

applications.evidence_summary: No published study of this product in this application located (PubMed search 2026-10-23: Bi-Ostetic calcaneus).
applications.caveats: Extremities named in the label.

evidence.title: Influence of 45S5 Bioactive Glass in A Standard Calcium Phosphate Collagen Bone Graft Substitute on the Posterolateral Fusion of Rabbit Spine
evidence.finding: Both mineralized collagen fillers (with and without 45S5 glass) showed normal healing and spine fusion comparable to iliac crest graft in rabbits.

bd.reimbursement: Bundled in MS-DRG inpatient; packaged in OPPS and ASC payment; no separate HCPCS code or pass-through for bone void fillers.
bd.notes: Small private company; no company page was read, and current commercial status rests on GUDID 'in commercial distribution' listings.

name: Bongros-HA / Bongros-GS (Korea)
ownership_history: CGBio (formerly Novomedics, Korea) also owns the Novosis rhBMP-2 record already in the atlas; Bioalpha as CGBio's subsidiary or partner is not confirmed.
composition: Synthetic hydroxyapatite bone chips (Bongros-HA) and related graft forms (Bongros-GS); Korean-market products.

regulatory.reference: No orthopedic 510(k) found. openFDA lists K090793 'BONGROS HA' (Bioalpha, Inc., May 2009) under dental product code LYC (not orthopedic MQV).
on_label_indications: Orthopedic spine and long-bone use is a Korean-market labeling; the only US record is a 2009 dental bone grafting clearance

applications.evidence_summary: Prospective, single-institution, case-matched intrapatient study of 32 instrumented PLF patients (Seoul): hydroxyapatite plus autograft on one side versus iliac autograft on the other, complete 3D-CT fusion 86.7% vs 88.9% at 12 months (not significant) (PMID 18615472).
applications.caveats: Korean institution, small n, side-by-side design; no US orthopedic clearance, so US use would be off-label or unauthorized.
applications.challenge: Do not present as US-available for orthopedics; the K090793 clearance is dental.

evidence.title: A prospective consecutive study of instrumented posterolateral lumbar fusion using synthetic hydroxyapatite (Bongros-HA) as a bone graft extender
